entries.9d46f74bf80c75972a42ae44acf1ed5848bf0bd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10851"/><div sID="gen19517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10851"/>19-21. This gives the reason why he gave way to the temptation to despair. The Margin, "Remember" does not suit the sense so well.<div eID="gen19517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wormwood ... gall--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.9.15">Jr 9:15</reference>). <div eID="gen19518" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd851f383de0e4615fb221d537c2b1393578a243: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10854"/><div sID="gen19522" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10854"/>22-24. (Mal 3:6). <div eID="gen19522" type="x-p"/>
entries.94ce04f95e072f59c81ef74f18582e7c64fda34e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10857"/><div sID="gen19526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10857"/>25-27. The repetition of "good" at the beginning of each of the three verses heightens the effect.<div eID="gen19526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wait--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.30.18">Is 30:18</reference>). <div eID="gen19527" type="x-p"/>
entries.566f87df430bd2e32794f15779a48597dcbbaf92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10860"/><div sID="gen19531" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10860"/>28-30. The fruit of true docility and patience. He does not fight against the yoke (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.18">Jr 31:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.5">Ac 9:5</reference>), but accommodates himself to it.<div eID="gen19531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alone--</hi>The heathen applauded magnanimity, but they looked to display and the praise of men. The child of God, in the absence of any witness, "alone," silently submits to the will of God.<div eID="gen19532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">borne it upon him--</hi>that is, because he is used to bearing it on him. Rather, "because He (the Lord, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.26">La 3:26</reference>) hath laid it on him" [Vatablus]. <div eID="gen19533" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a9ece71db112794694b2c3a2b538ea60b798294: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10863"/><div sID="gen19538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10863"/>31-33. True repentance is never without hope (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.14">Psa 94:14</reference>). <div eID="gen19538" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb300fd48ffc4c84906b3507f2c2106c500c978a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10866"/><div sID="gen19542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10866"/>34-36. This triplet has an infinitive in the beginning of each verse, the governing finite verb being in the end of <reference osisRef="Lam.3.36">La 3:36</reference>, "the Lord approveth not," which is to be repeated in each verse. Jeremiah here anticipates and answers the objections which the Jews might start, that it was by His connivance they were "crushed under the feet" of those who "turned aside the right of a man." God approves (literally, "seeth," <reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Ha 1:13</reference>; so "behold," "look on," that is, look on with approval) not of such unrighteous acts; and so the Jews may look for deliverance and the punishment of their foes. <div eID="gen19542" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d25e99c0643116a0a73e972cfc5b34738ce23ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10869"/><div sID="gen19546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10869"/>37-39. Who is it that can (as God, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.9">Psa 33:9</reference>) effect by a word anything, without the will of God? <div eID="gen19546" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1c02c4755397e5329ab506be380ed58986a5a0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10872"/><div sID="gen19551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10872"/><hi type="bold">40-42. us--</hi>Jeremiah and his fellow countrymen in their calamity.<div eID="gen19551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">search--</hi>as opposed to the torpor wherewith men rest only on their outward sufferings, without attending to the cause of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.23">Psa 139:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen19552" type="x-p"/>
entries.942e3517b75eec48c5a3637bf31de2bd59e7f1ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10875"/><div sID="gen19556" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10875"/><hi type="bold">43-45. covered--</hi>namely, thyself (so <reference osisRef="Lam.3.44">La 3:44</reference>), so as not to see and pity our calamities, for even the most cruel in seeing a sad spectacle are moved to pity. Compare as to God "hiding His face," <reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.25">22:25</reference>. <div eID="gen19556" type="x-p"/>
entries.e520d5f0aebefdab8dd81978dd5a0bf35427416a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10878"/><div sID="gen19560" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10878"/>46-48. Pe is put before Ain (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.43">La 3:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.46">46</reference>), as in <reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">La 2:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.16">4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">17</reference>. (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">La 2:16</reference>.) <div eID="gen19560" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8e24dfa772a4991065c0d7a8e14d4c9de97e937: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10881"/><div sID="gen19564" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10881"/><hi type="bold">49-51. without ... intermission--</hi>or else, "because there is no intermission" [Piscator], namely, of my miseries. <div eID="gen19564" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d48293c6d7062399693427973aa342d8b179040: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10884"/><div sID="gen19570" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10884"/><hi type="bold">52-54. a bird--</hi>which is destitute of counsel and strength. The allusion seems to be to <reference osisRef="Prov.1.17">Pr 1:17</reference> [Calvin].<div eID="gen19570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19571" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without cause--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">Psa 69:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.3">109:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">4</reference>). Type of Messiah (<reference osisRef="John.15.25">Joh 15:25</reference>). <div eID="gen19571" type="x-p"/>
entries.981aad9d9f273ce6ba3dd111795391fb8c093d32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10887"/><div sID="gen19577" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10887"/><hi type="bold">55-57. I called out of dungeon--</hi>Thus the spirit resists the flesh, and faith spurns the temptation [Calvin], (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.1">Psa 130:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">Jon 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen19577" type="x-p"/>
entries.9eb8f2e35a421126f56a1ef3941876fb5dd4a4c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10890"/><div sID="gen19582" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10890"/>58-60. Jeremiah cites God's gracious answers to his prayers as an encouragement to his fellow countrymen, to trust in Him.<div eID="gen19582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19583" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleaded--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.35.1">Psa 35:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">Mi 7:9</reference>). <div eID="gen19583" type="x-p"/>
entries.44762b42293ef86736a9ad0eea23ed02fdcfa8f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10893"/><div sID="gen19588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10893"/><hi type="bold">61-63. their reproach--</hi>their reproachful language against me. <div eID="gen19588" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a30bc1239557b73eb1da2c440187c5c6428bb68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10896"/><div sID="gen19592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10896"/>64-66. (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.20">Jr 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.14">2Ti 4:14</reference>). <div eID="gen19592" type="x-p"/>

entries.ffb818a6d513e5482e95ef03fda33784eb8c157b: <div eID="gen31010" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31011" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31012" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31012" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31011" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31013" type="x-p"/> The prophet, by enumerating his own severe trials, vv. 1-20, and showing his trust in God, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.21">Lam 3:21</reference>, encourages his people to the like resignation and trust in the Divine and never-failing mercy, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.22-Lam.3.27">Lam 3:22-27</reference>. He vindicates the goodness of God in all his dispensations, and the unreasonableness of murmuring under them, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.28-Lam.3.39">Lam 3:28-39</reference>. He recommends self-examination and repentance; and then, from their experience of former deliverances from God, encourages them to look for pardon for their sins, and retribution to their enemies, vv. 40-66. <div eID="gen31013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31014" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31015" type="x-p"/> I am the man that hath seen affliction - Either the prophet speaks here of himself, or he is personating his miserable countrymen. This and other passages in this poem have been applied to Jesus Christ's passion; but, in my opinion, without any foundation.
entries.2fd7de66d88cab87cfeddb8a4e5e0fd643d49bf2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31016" type="x-p"/> He hath - brought me into darkness - In the sacred writings, darkness is often taken for calamity, light, for prosperity.
entries.1def16cb6edbdd8f9aa51afd0c697be6de7bdcd0: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31017" type="x-p"/> He hath builded against me - Perhaps there is a reference here to the mounds and ramparts raised by the Chaldeans in order to take the city.
entries.89bb3814b3af5e34259a009b18e5309590ba6cd7: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31018" type="x-p"/> He hath hedged me about - This also may refer to the lines drawn round the city during the siege. But these and similar expressions in the following verses may be merely metaphorical, to point out their straitened, oppressed, and distressed state.
entries.25a78f60307867029322c464a265939e7c758f05: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31019" type="x-p"/> He hath inclosed my ways with hewn stone - He has put insuperable obstacles in my way; and confounded all my projects of deliverance and all my expectations of prosperity.
entries.d2f25ff697cba2bcbcebf1871d0142978f8659be: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen31019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31020" type="x-p"/> He hath bent his bow, and set me as a mark for the arrow - One might conjecture that the following thought in the Toozek i Teemour was borrowed from this: - "One addressed the caliph Aaly, and said, 'If the heavens were a bow, and the earth the cord thereof; if calamities were arrows, man the butt for those arrows; and the holy blessed God the unerring marksman; where could the sons of Adam flee for succor?' The caliph replied, 'The children of Adam must flee unto the Lord.'" This was the state of poor Jerusalem. It seemed as a butt for all God's arrows; and each arrow of calamity entered into the soul, for God was the unerring marksman.
entries.35495a842cae96f42b4196081e946febf1153ecb: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31021" type="x-p"/> The arrows of his quiver - בני אשפתו beney ashpatho, "The sons of his quiver." The issue or effect; the subject, adjunct, or accident, or produce of a thing, is frequently denominated its son or child. So arrows that issue from a quiver are here termed the sons of the quiver.
entries.ec627746d44adca294eedc1ead3273ae2ed68e98: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen31021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31022" type="x-p"/> He hath filled me with bitterness - במרורים bimrorim, with bitternesses, bitter upon bitter. <div eID="gen31022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31023" type="x-p"/> He hath made me drunken with wormwood - I have drunk the cup of misery till I am intoxicated with it. Almost in all countries, and in all languages, bitterness is a metaphor to express trouble and affliction. The reason is, there is nothing more disagreeable to the taste than the one; and nothing more distressing to the mind than the other. An Arabic poet. Amralkeis, one of the writers of the Moallakat, terms a man grievously afflicted a pounder of wormwood.
entries.9974027a50e8593b3e3b258021465938c54a0ce5: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen31023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31024" type="x-p"/> He hath also broken my teeth with gravel stones - What a figure to express disgust, pain, and the consequent incapacity of taking food for the support of life; a man, instead of bread, being obliged to eat small pebbles till all his teeth are broken to pieces by endeavoring to grind them. One can scarcely read this description without feeling the toothache. The next figure is not less expressive. <div eID="gen31024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31025" type="x-p"/> He hath covered me with ashes - הכפישני באפר hichphishani beepher, "he hath plunged me into the dust." To be thrown into a mass or bed of perfect dust, where the eyes are blinded by it, the ears stopped, and the mouth and lungs filled at the very first attempt to respire after having been thrown into it - what a horrible idea of suffocation and drowning! One can scarcely read this without feeling a suppression of breath, or a stricture upon the lungs! Did ever man paint sorrow like this man?
entries.6c68e798ce1688b3368a03c33f140dc78b408d5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen31025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31026" type="x-p"/> Those hast removed my soul - Prosperity is at such an utter distance from me, that it is impossible I should ever reach it; and as to happiness, I have forgotten whether I have ever tasted of it.
entries.5f36cf782fc5699d5c36c779fbc2b08fcb12877f: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen31026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31027" type="x-p"/> And my hope - That first, that last support of the miserable - it is gone! it is perished! The sovereign God alone can revive it.
entries.84bfe3c05b7632c480ec85f9161b80214091fc81: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen31027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31028" type="x-p"/> By soul - is humbled in me - It is evident that in the preceding verses there is a bitterness of complaint against the bitterness of adversity, that is not becoming to man when under the chastising hand of God; and, while indulging this feeling, all hope fled. Here we find a different feeling; he humbles himself under the mighty hand of God, and then his hope revives, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.21">Lam 3:21</reference>.
entries.176ebd0952539134cbcf54f95ed84853e3cc95c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen31028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31029" type="x-p"/> It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed - Being thus humbled, and seeing himself and his sinfulness in a proper point of view, he finds that God, instead of dealing with him in judgment, has dealt with him in mercy; and that though the affliction was excessive, yet it seas less than his iniquity deserved. If, indeed, any sinner be kept out of hell, it is because God's compassion faileth not.
entries.e03f3a234f7922b1aa8f8a96a673243b376595c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen31029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31030" type="x-p"/> They are new every morning - Day and night proclaim the mercy and compassion of God. Who could exist throughout the day, if there were not a continual superintending Providence? Who could be preserved in the night, if the Watchman of Israel ever slumbered or slept?
entries.1e7e46d4a0c1c4396290579d86bf7ba42e587c20: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen31030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31031" type="x-p"/> The Lord is my portion - See on <reference osisRef="Psa.119.67">Psa 119:67</reference> (note).
entries.cd1f1e33c748f258d338d5bab8aca09c091ff3f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen31031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31032" type="x-p"/> It is good that a man should both hope - Hope is essentially necessary to faith; he that hopes not, cannot believe; if there be no expectation, there can be no confidence. When a man hopes for salvation, he should not only waft for it, but use every means that may lead to it; for hope cannot live, if there be no exercise. If hope become impatient, faith will be impossible: for who can believe for his salvation when his mind is agitated? He must therefore quietly wait. He must expect, and yet be dumb, as the words imply; ever feeling his utter unworthiness; and, without murmuring, struggle into life.
entries.c3396c1084967294e0570900ed993b3fead1b639: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen31032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31033" type="x-p"/> That he bear the yoke in his youth - Early habits, when good, are invaluable. Early discipline is equally so. He who has not got under wholesome restraint in youth will never make a useful man, a good man, nor a happy man.
entries.0512e3d22a483636b2bae75295b3f9f61d53b3e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen31033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31034" type="x-p"/> He sitteth alone - He has learned that necessary lesson of independence, that shows him how he is to serve himself; to give no trouble to others; and keep his troubles, as far as possible, in his own bosom.
entries.6a68afb7109845109e09e7538f94301b988ec174: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen31034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31035" type="x-p"/> He putteth his mouth in the dust - Lives in a state of deep humility. <div eID="gen31035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31036" type="x-p"/> If so be there may be hope - Because there is room for hope.
entries.229c6cae4216f171d5e837fea17df465776ca657: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen31036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31037" type="x-p"/> He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth - He has that love that is not provoked. He is not quarrelsome, nor apt to resent injuries; he suffers long and is kind. Or, it may be rendered, "let him give his cheek." <div eID="gen31037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31038" type="x-p"/> He is filled full with reproach - Though all this take place, yet let his "trust be in God, who will not cast off for ever." God will take his part, and bring him safely through all hardships.
entries.69288f0f185077fd3992981e01a26f1ec82a2256: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen31038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31039" type="x-p"/> The Lord - אדני Adonai; but one of my ancient MSS. has יהוה Jehovah. The above verse is quoted in reference to our Lord's passion, by <reference osisRef="Mat.26.62">Mat 26:62</reference>.
entries.ed0aa6621485308c7b0e33d2fbbb5fe8ccc86984: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen31039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31040" type="x-p"/> For he doth not afflict willingly - It is no pleasure to God to afflict men. He takes no delight in our pain and misery: yet, like a tender and intelligent parent, he uses the rod; not to gratify himself, but to profit and save us.
entries.07808c1b270a73e829e0a44e96368b455534b030: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen31040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31041" type="x-p"/> To crush under his feet - He can neither gain credit nor pleasure in trampling upon those who are already bound, and in suffering; such he knows to be the state of man here below. From which it most assuredly follows, that God never afflicts us but for our good, nor chastises but that we may be partakers of his holiness. <div eID="gen31041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31042" type="x-p"/> All the prisoners of the earth - By the prisoners of the earth, or land, Dr. Blayney understands those insolvent debtors who were put in prison, and there obliged to work out the debt. Yet this is mercy in comparison with those who put them in prison, and keep them there, when they know that it is impossible, from the state of the laws, to lessen the debt by their confinement. <div eID="gen31042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31043" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Lam.3.34">Lam 3:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.35">Lam 3:35</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lam.3.36">Lam 3:36</reference>, certain acts of tyranny, malice, and injustice are specified, which men often indulge themselves in the practice of towards one another, but which the Divine goodness is far from countenancing or approving by any similar conduct. - Blayney.
entries.782889eb45464361d9470812c0c3c8c632a85450: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen31043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31044" type="x-p"/> To turn aside the right of a man - To make a man lose his right, because one of the higher orders opposes him. Dr. Blayney thinks that עליון elyon, instead of being referred to God, should be considered as pointing out one of the chief of the people. I do not see that we gain any thing by this. The evil fact is, turning aside the right of a man; and the aggravation of it is, doing it before the face of the Most High; that is, in a court of justice, where God is ever considered to be present.
entries.9f6052ea9e15d082ba71724b2eef9ba80c4d14fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen31044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31045" type="x-p"/> To subvert a man in his cause - To prevent his having justice done him in a lawsuit, etc., by undue interference, as by suborning false witnesses, or exerting any kind of influence in opposition to truth and right. - Blayney. <div eID="gen31045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31046" type="x-p"/> The Lord approved not - Instead of אדני Adonai, seventeen MSS., of Kennicott's, and one ancient of my own, have יהוה Yehovah. Approveth not, לא ראה lo raah, doth not see, turns away his face from it, abhors it.
entries.e31035ca55a3d84ad31f9f00796949ed5b27f2c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen31046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31047" type="x-p"/> Wherefore doth a living man complain - He who has his life still lent to him has small cause of complaint. How great soever his affliction may be, he is still alive; therefore, he may seek and find mercy unto eternal life. Of this, death would deprive him; therefore let not a living man complain.
entries.8a4433b78f4a7569996445882758c91d02ad0045: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen31047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31048" type="x-p"/> Let us search - How are we to get the pardon of our sins? The prophet tells us: <div eID="gen31048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31049" type="x-p"/> 1. Let us examine ourselves. <div eID="gen31049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31050" type="x-p"/> 2. "Let us turn again to the Lord." <div eID="gen31050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31051" type="x-p"/> 3. "Let us lift up our heart;" let us make fervent prayer and supplication for mercy. <div eID="gen31051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31052" type="x-p"/> 4. "Let us lift up our hand;" let us solemnly promise to be his, and bind ourselves in a covenant to be the Lord's only: so much lifting up the hand to God implies. Or, let us put our heart on our hand, and offer it to God; so some have translated this clause. <div eID="gen31052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31053" type="x-p"/> 5. "We have transgressed;" let our confession of sin be fervent and sincere. <div eID="gen31053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31054" type="x-p"/> 6. And to us who profess Christianity it may be added, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ as having died for thee; and thou shalt not perish, but have everlasting life. <reference osisRef="Lam.3.46">Lam 3:46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.47">Lam 3:47</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.48">Lam 3:48</reference>, beginning with פ phe, should, as to the order of the alphabet, follow <reference osisRef="Lam.3.49">Lam 3:49</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.50">Lam 3:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.51">Lam 3:51</reference>, which begin with ע ain, which in its grammatical position precedes the former.
entries.6031d9c7fedd0100fae92cc3be1cca2156a55bef: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen31054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31055" type="x-p"/> Fear and a snare - See on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.13">Jer 48:13</reference> (note).
entries.134e861ecf2812e2b7a2d394de5a5e5e81a0e68f: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen31055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31056" type="x-p"/> Mine eye runneth down - I weep incessantly.
entries.6d339eb65fbfd9ae20f3b3320ada22914de2abd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 51</hi> <div eID="gen31056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31057" type="x-p"/> Mine eye affecteth mine heart - What I see I feel. I see nothing but misery; and I feel, in consequence, nothing but pain. There have been various translations of the original: but they all amount to this. <div eID="gen31057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31058" type="x-p"/> The daughters of my city - The villages about Jerusalem.
entries.9c4f869f630a8555eae9f80f5e11e0b69003bbc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 52</hi> <div eID="gen31058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31059" type="x-p"/> Mine enemies chased me - From this to the end of the chapter the prophet speaks of his own personal sufferings, and especially of those which he endured in the dungeon. See <reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">Jer 38:6</reference>, etc.
entries.4340f77b9a97d4dfa3afbcf5b3d1da70880c035a: <hi type="bold">Verse 56</hi> <div eID="gen31059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31060" type="x-p"/> Hide not thine ear at my breathing - He dared not even to complain, nor to cry, nor to pray aloud: he was obliged to whisper his prayer to God. It was only a breathing.
entries.59f43db6e20fa0adc5c5f7a5e84e66521d8d1d1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 57</hi> <div eID="gen31060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31061" type="x-p"/> Fear not - How powerful is this word when spoken by the Spirit of the Lord to a disconsolate heart. To every mourner we may say, on the authority of God, Fear not! God will plead thy cause, and redeem thy soul.
entries.253461c0ee4f9cd23c1118fb32b9a998ddb9e412: <hi type="bold">Verse 60</hi> <div eID="gen31061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31062" type="x-p"/> Thou hast seen - all their imaginations - Every thing is open to the eye of God. Distressed soul! though thou knowest not what thy enemies meditate against thee; yet he who loves thee does, and will infallibly defeat all their plots, and save thee.
entries.7cefb64f753440a1a56dd55c8c5b197933a07b60: <hi type="bold">Verse 65</hi> <div eID="gen31062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31063" type="x-p"/> Give them sorrow of heart - They shall have a callous heart, covered with obstinacy, and thy execration. The former is their state, the latter their fate. This is the consequence of their hardening their hearts from thy fear. Blayney translates, "Thou wilt give with a hearty concordance thy curse unto them." That is, Thou wilt give it to them freely, and without reserve; intimating that God felt no longer any bowels of compassion for them. Formerly he inflicted punishments with reluctance, while there was any hope of amendment: but, in the instance before us, the case was so hopeless, that God acts according to the simple principle of vindictive justice. The prophet therefore considers them on the utmost verge of final reprobation: another plunge, and they are lost for ever.
entries.4dda90ca77df0e8a9f5cd3cebfc46f9d17f916bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 66</hi> <div eID="gen31063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31064" type="x-p"/> Persecute and destroy them - Thou wilt pursue them with destruction. These are all declaratory, not imprecatory. <div eID="gen31064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31065" type="x-p"/> From under the heavens of the Lord - This verse seems to allude to the Chaldaic prediction, in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.11">Jer 10:11</reference>. By their conduct they will bring on themselves the curse denounced against their enemies. <div eID="gen31065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31066" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint and Vulgate seem to have read "From under heaven, O Jehovah:" and the Syriac reads, "Thy heavens, O Jehovah!" None of these makes any material change in the meaning of the words. <div eID="gen31066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31067" type="x-p"/> It has already been noticed in the introduction, that this chapter contains a triple acrostic, three lines always beginning with the same letter; so that the Hebrew alphabet is thrice repeated in this chapter, twenty-two multiplied by three being equal to sixty-six.  <chapter eID="Lam.3"/> <div eID="gen31067" type="x-p"/>

entries.9d18bed273c32b6c560cb97f1ab8125d1d0170c2: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.1-Lam.3.66">Lamentations 3:1-66</reference> <div eID="gen14675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14676" type="x-p"/> The two preceding poems ended with sorrowful complaint. This third poem begins with the complaint of a man over grievous personal suffering. Regarding the contents of this poem, and its relation to the two which precede, Ewald makes the following excellent remarks: "In consequence of experiences most peculiarly his own, the individual may indeed at first make complaint, in such a way that, as here, still deeper despair for the third time begins (vv. 1-18); but, by the deepest meditation for himself on the eternal relation of God to men, he may also very readily come to the due acknowledgment of his own sins and the necessity for repentance, and thereby also to believing prayer. Who is this individual that complains, and thinks, and entreats in this fashion, whose <hi type="italic">I</hi> passes unobserved, but quite appropriately, into <hi type="italic">we</hi>? O man, it is the very image of thyself! Every one must now speak and think as he does. Thus it is just by this address, which commences in the most doleful tones, that sorrow for the first time, and imperceptibly, has passed into true prayer." This remark contains both the deepest truth and the key to the proper understanding of the contents of this poem, and its position in the middle of the Lamentations. Both of these points have been mistaken by expositors, who (e.g., C. B. Michaelis, Pareau, Maurer, Kalkschmidt, and Bleek in his <hi type="italic">Introduction</hi>) are of opinion that the writer here makes his personal sufferings the subject of complaint. This cannot be made out, either from <reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">Lam 3:14</reference> or from the description given in Lam 3:53.: the reverse rather is shown by the fact that, in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.22">Lam 3:22</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lam.3.40-Lam.3.47">Lam 3:40-47</reference>, <hi type="italic">we</hi> is used instead of <hi type="italic">I</hi>; from which it is evident that the prophet, in the remainder of the poem, is not speaking of himself, or bewailing his own personal sufferings. The confession found in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.42">Lam 3:42</reference>, "We have transgressed and rebelled, Thou hast not pardoned," etc., necessarily presupposes not only that the dealing of God towards the sinful and apostate nation, as described in Lam 3:42., stands in the closest connection with the sufferings of which the prophet complains in vv. 1-18, but also that the chastisement, by means of God’s wrath, which was experienced by the man who utters his complaint in vv. 1-18, is identical with the anger which, according to <reference osisRef="Lam.3.43">Lam 3:43</reference>, discharged itself on the people; hence the suffering of the individual, which is described in vv. 1-18, is to be regarded as the reflex of but a special instance of the suffering endured by the whole community. Perhaps this was the view of Aben Ezra, when he says that, in this lamentation, it is individual Israelites who speak; and most expositors acknowledge that the prophet pours forth his lamentations and his prayers in the name of the godly. <div eID="gen14676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14677" type="x-p"/> The poem begins by setting forth the grievous soul-sufferings of the godly in their cheerless and hopeless misery (vv. 1-18); then it ascends, through meditation upon the compassion and almighty providence of God, to hope (vv. 19-39), and thus attains to the recognition of God’s justice in sending the punishment, which, however, is so intensified through the malice of enemies, that the Lord cannot pass by the attempt to crush His people (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.40-Lam.3.54">Lam 3:40-54</reference>). This reliance on the justice of God impels to prayer, in which there is manifested confidence that God will send help, and take vengeance on the enemy (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.55-Lam.3.66">Lam 3:55-66</reference>). <div eID="gen14677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14678" type="x-p"/> Lamentation over grievous sufferings. The author of these sufferings is not, indeed, expressly named in the whole section, but it is unmistakeably signified that God is meant; moreover, at the end of <reference osisRef="Lam.3.18">Lam 3:18</reference> the name יהוה is mentioned. The view thus given of the sufferings shows, not merely that he who utters the complaint perceives in these sufferings a chastisement by God, but also that this chastisement has become for him a soul-struggle, in which he may not take the name of God into his mouth; and only after he has given vent in lamentations to the deep sorrow of his soul, does his spirit get peace to mention the name of the Lord, and make complaint to Him of his need. Nothing certain can be inferred from the lamentations themselves regarding the person who makes complaint. It does not follow from <reference osisRef="Lam.3.1-Lam.3.3">Lam 3:1-3</reference> that he was burdened with sorrows more than every one else; nor from <reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">Lam 3:14</reference> that he was a personage well known to all the people, so that one could recognise the prophet in him. As little are they sufferings which Jeremiah has endured alone, and for his own sake, but sufferings such as many godly people of his time have undergone and struggled through. Against the Jeremianic authorship of the poem, therefore, no argument can be drawn from the fact that the personality of him who utters the complaint is concealed. <div eID="gen14678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14679" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.1">Lam 3:1</reference> <div eID="gen14679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14680" type="x-p"/> In the complaint, "I am the man that saw (i.e., lived to see) misery," the misery is not specified; and we cannot, with Rosenmüller, refer עני (without the article) to the misery announced by the prophet long before. "The rod of His wrath," as in <reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Pro 22:8</reference>, is the rod of God’s anger; cf. <reference osisRef="Job.21.9">Job 21:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Isa 10:5</reference>, etc. The suffix in עברתו is not to be referred, with Aben Ezra, to the enemy.
entries.b2e315f0c0b18b9776f15fdd71cacfc104504857: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.2">Lam 3:2</reference> "Me hath He (God) led and brought through darkness (חשׁך, local accus.), and not light," is a combination like that in <reference osisRef="Job.12.25">Job 12:25</reference> and Amo 5:18. The path of Jeremiah’s life certainly lay through darkness, but was not wholly devoid of light, because God had promised him His protection for the discharge of his official functions. The complaint applies to all the godly, to whom, at the fall of Jerusalem, no light appeared to cheer the darkness of life’s pathway.
entries.0f69f3d92a396d52b32e4b0f825df02ea4b0476e: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.3-Lam.3.5">Lam 3:3-5</reference> "Only upon (against) me does He repeatedly turn His hand." ישׁוּב is subordinated to the idea of יהפך in an adverbial sense; cf. Gesenius, §142, 3, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. "His hand" is the smiting hand of God. אך, "<hi type="italic">only</hi> upon me," expresses the feeling which makes him on whom grievous sufferings have fallen to regard himself as one smitten in a special manner by God. "The whole day," i.e., continually; cf. Lam 1:13. - From <reference osisRef="Lam.3.4">Lam 3:4</reference> onwards this divine chastisement is more minutely set forth under various figures, and first of all as a wasting away of the vital force. בּלּה means to wear out by rubbing, cause to fall away, from בּלה, to be worn out, which is applied to clothes, and then transferred to bodies, <reference osisRef="Job.13.28">Job 13:28</reference>; Psa 49:15. "Flesh and skin" are the exterior and soft constituents of the body, while the bones are the firmer parts. Skin, flesh, and bones together, make up the substance of the human body. <reference osisRef="Prov.5.11">Pro 5:11</reference> forms the foundation of the first clause. "He hath broken my bones" is a reminiscence from the lamentation of Hezekiah in <reference osisRef="Isa.38.13">Isa 38:13</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.10">Psa 51:10</reference>; Job 30:17. The meaning is thus excellently given by Pareau: <hi type="italic">indicantur animi, fortius irae divinae malorumque sensu conquassati, angores</hi>. - The figure in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.5">Lam 3:5</reference>, "He builds round about and encircles me," is derived from the enclosing of a city by besieging it. עלי is to be repeated after wayaqeep. The besieging forces, which encompass him so that he cannot go out and in, are ראשׁ וּתלאה. That the former of these two words cannot mean κεφαλήν μου (lxx), is abundantly evident. ראשׁ or רושׁ is a plant with a very bitter taste, hence a poisonous plant; see on Jer 8:14. As in that passage מי ראשׁ, so here the simple ראשׁ is an emblem of bitter suffering. The combination with תּלאה, "toil," is remarkable, as a case in which a figurative is joined with a literal expression; this, however, does not justify the change of תּלאה into לענה (Castell, Schleussner, etc.). The combination is to be explained on the ground that ראשׁ had become so common a symbol of bitter suffering, that the figure was quite lost sight of behind the thing signified.
entries.e14873b375dcf34b06b0ba47489d709ddf21ab7c: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.6">Lam 3:6</reference> <div eID="gen14680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14681" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.6">Lam 3:6</reference> is a <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> reminiscence from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">Psa 143:3</reference></hi>. מחשׁכּים is the darkness of the grave and of Sheol; cf. Psa 88:7. מתי עולם does not mean "the dead of antiquity" (Rosenmüller, Maurer, Ewald, Thenius, etc.), but, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">Psa 143:3</reference>, those eternally dead, who lie in the long night of death, from which there is no return into this life. In opposition to the explanation <hi type="italic">dudum mortui</hi>, Gerlach fittingly remarks, that "it makes no difference whether they have been dead long ago or only recently, inasmuch as those dead and buried a short time ago lie in darkness equally with those who have long been dead;" while it avails nothing to point to <reference osisRef="Ps.88.5-Ps.88.7">Psa 88:5-7</reference>, as Nägelsbach does, since the special subject there treated of is not those who have <hi type="italic">long</hi> been dead.
entries.4a005f97514f9c95a7f23b546146882e9940f31c: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.7">Lam 3:7</reference> <div eID="gen14681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14682" type="x-p"/> God has hedged him round like a prisoner, cut off all communication from without, so that he cannot escape, and He has loaded him with heavy chains. This figure is based on <reference osisRef="Job.19.8">Job 19:8</reference> and Hos 2:8. גּדר בּעדי, "He hath made an hedge round me," does not suggest prison walls, but merely seclusion within a confined space, where he is deprived of free exit. "I cannot go out," as in Psa 88:9. The seclusion is increased by fetters which are placed on the prisoner. נחשׁת, "brass," for fetters, as in German and English, "irons," for iron chains.
entries.8f1865cc1dc60bb386f5b93a624eeaa744931e5a: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.8">Lam 3:8</reference> <div eID="gen14682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14683" type="x-p"/> This distress presses upon him all the more heavily, because, in addition to this, the Lord does not listen to his prayer and cries, but has rather closed His ear; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jer 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.42">Psa 18:42</reference>, etc. שׂתם for סתם (only written here with שׂ), to stop the prayer; i.e., not to prevent the prayer from issuing out of the breast, to restrain supplication, but to prevent the prayer from reaching His ear; cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.3.44">Lam 3:44</reference> and Pro 1:28.
entries.b1580b2b597a7d1520d9a3db1b858e4635c3e7c6: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.9">Lam 3:9</reference> <div eID="gen14683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14684" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Lam.3.9">Lam 3:9</reference>, the idea of prevention from freedom of action is further carried out on a new side. "He hath walled in my paths with hewn stones." גּזית = גזית  אבּני, 1 Kings 5:31, are hewn stones of considerable size, employed for making a very strong wall. The meaning is: He has raised up insurmountable obstacles in the pathway of my life. "My paths hath He turned," i.e., rendered such that I cannot walk in them. עוּה is to turn, in the sense of destroying, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">Isa 24:1</reference>, not <hi type="italic">contortas fecit</hi> (Michaelis, Rosenmüller, Kalkschmidt), nor <hi type="italic">per viam tortuosam ire cogor</hi> (Raschi); for the prophet does not mean to say (as Nägelsbach imagines), "that he has been compelled to walk in wrong and tortuous ways," but he means that God has rendered it impossible for him to proceed further in his path; cf. Job 30:13. But we are not in this to think of the levelling of a raised road, as Thenius does; for נתיבה does not mean a road formed by the deposition of rubbish, like a mound, but a footpath, formed by constant treading (Gerlach).
entries.929f0a913b782946f2aa5b698f6c3038258099a5: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.10-Lam.3.11">Lam 3:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen14684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14685" type="x-p"/> Not merely, however, has God cut off every way of escape for him who here utters the complaint, but He pursues him in every possible way, that He may utterly destroy him. On the figure of a bear lying in wait, cf. Hos 13:8; Amo 5:19. It is more usual to find enemies compared to lions in ambush; cf. Ps. 10:19; Psa 17:12. The last-named passage seems to have been present to the writer’s mind. The prophets frequently compare enemies to lions, e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.5.6">Jer 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.7">Jer 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jer 49:19</reference>; Jer 50:44. - In <reference osisRef="Lam.3.11">Lam 3:11</reference> the figure of the lion is discontinued; for cowreer דּרכי cannot be said of a beast. The verb here is not to be derived from סרר, to be refractory, but is the Pilel of סוּר, to go aside, deviate, make to draw back. To "make ways turn aside" may signify to make a person lose the right road, but not to drag back from the road (Thenius); it rather means to mislead, or even <hi type="italic">facere ut deficiant viae</hi>, to take away the road, so that one cannot escape. פּשּׁח is ἅπ. λεγ. in Hebrew; in Aramean it means to cut or tear in pieces: cf. [the Targum on] <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.33">1Sa 15:33</reference>, "Samuel  פּשּׁח Agag," hewed him in pieces; and on <reference osisRef="Ps.7.3">Psa 7:3</reference>, where the word is used for the Heb. פּרק, to tear in pieces (of a lion); here it signifies to tear away (limbs from the body, boughs from trees). This meaning is required by the context; for the following expression, שׂמני שׁומם, does not lead us to think of tearing in pieces, lacerating, but <hi type="italic">discerpere</hi>, plucking or pulling to pieces. For שׁומם, see on <reference osisRef="Lam.1.13">Lam 1:13</reference>, Lam 1:16.
entries.5df7fcff1e96203239e80b254202cbeab278e1a9: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.12-Lam.3.13">Lam 3:12-13</reference> "He hath bent His bow," as in Lam 2:4. The second member, "He hath made me the mark for His arrows," is taken almost <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> from Job 16:12. The arrows are the ills and sorrows appointed by God; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.23">Deu 32:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">Psa 38:3</reference>; Job 6:4.
entries.4354fe8c82cc0723cff66950827d82b412a3ea0b: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">Lam 3:14</reference> "Abused in this way, he is the object of scoffing and mockery" (Gerlach). In the first clause, the complaint of Jeremiah in <reference osisRef="Jer.20.7">Jer 20:7</reference> is reproduced. Rosenmüller, Ewald, and Thenius are inclined to take עמּי as an abbreviated form of the plur. עמּים, presuming that the subject of the complaint is the people of Israel. But in none of the three passages in which Ewald (<hi type="italic">Gram</hi>. §177, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), following the Masoretes, is ready to recognise such a plural-ending, does there seem any need or real foundation for the assumption. Besides this passage, the others are <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.44">2Sa 22:44</reference> and Psa 144:2. In these last two cases עמּי gives a suitable enough meaning as a singular (see the expositions of these passages); and in this verse, as Gerlach has already remarked, against Rosenmüller, neither the conjoined כּל nor the plural suffix of נגינתם requires us to take עמּי as a plural, the former objection being removed on a comparison of <reference osisRef="Gen.41.10">Gen 41:10</reference>, and the latter when we consider the possibility of a <hi type="italic">constructio ad sensum</hi> in the case of the collective עם. But the assumption that here the people are speaking, or that the poet (prophet) is complaining of the sufferings of the people in their name, is opposed by the fact that הגּבר stands at the beginning of this lamentation, Lam 3:1. If, however, the prophet complained in the name of each individual among God’s people, he could not set up כּל־עמּי in opposition to them, because by that very expression the scoffing is limited to the great body of the people. The Chaldee, accordingly, is substantially correct in its paraphrase, <hi type="italic">omnibus protervis populi mei</hi> (following <reference osisRef="Dan.11.14">Dan 11:14</reference>). But that the mass of the people were not subdued by suffering, and that there was a great number of those who would not recognise the chastening hand of God in the fall of the kingdom, and who scoffed at the warnings of the prophets, is evinced, not merely by the history of the period immediately after the destruction of Jerusalem (Jer. 41ff.), and by the conduct of Ishmael and his followers (Jer 41:2.), and of the insolent men who marched to Egypt in spite of Jeremiah’s warning (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.2">Jer 43:2</reference>), but also by the spirit that prevailed among the exiles, and against which Ezekiel had to contend; cf. e.g., Eze 12:22. נגינתם is a reminiscence from <reference osisRef="Job.30.9">Job 30:9</reference>; cf. Psa 69:13.
entries.6258571c124c563455f32e6d27fcf34880417fd4: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.15-Lam.3.16">Lam 3:15-16</reference> "He fills me with bitternesses" is a reminiscence from <reference osisRef="Job.9.18">Job 9:18</reference>, only ממרורים being exchanged for מרורים. Of these two forms, the first occurs only in Job, <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>; the latter denotes, in <reference osisRef="Exod.12.8">Exo 12:8</reference> and Num 9:11, "bitter herbs," but here "bitternesses." The reality (viz., bitter sorrow) is what Jeremiah threatens the people with in <reference osisRef="Jer.9.14">Jer 9:14</reference>; Jer 23:15. The figure employed in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.16">Lam 3:16</reference> is still stronger. "He made my teeth be ground down on gravel." חצץ means a gravel stone, gravel, Pro 20:17. גּרס (which occurs only in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.20">Psa 119:20</reference> as well as here, and is allied to גּרשׂ, from which comes גּרשׂ, something crushed, <reference osisRef="Lev.2.14">Lev 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.2.16">Lev 2:16</reference>) signifies to be ground down, and in Hiphil to grind down, <hi type="italic">not</hi> to cause to grind; hence בּחצץ cannot be taken as a second object, "He made my teeth grind gravel" (Ewald); but the words simply mean, "He ground my teeth on the gravel," i.e., He made them grind away on the gravel. As regards the application of the words, we cannot follow the older expositors in thinking of bread mixed with stones, but must view the giving of stones for bread as referring to cruel treatment. The lxx have rendered הכפּישׁני by ἐψώμισέν με σποδόν, the Vulgate by <hi type="italic">cibavit me cinere</hi>. This translation has not been lexically established, but is a mere conjecture from Psa 102:10. The ἁπ λεγ. ̔́̔̀נבך̓̀צ is allied with  ,כּבשׁ<hi type="italic">subigere</hi>, and means in Rabbinic, <hi type="italic">deprimere</hi>; cf. Buxtorf, <hi type="italic">Lex. Rabb. s.v.</hi> Similarly, the Chaldee had previously explained the words to mean <hi type="italic">humiliavit</hi> ( )כּנע<hi type="italic">me in cinere</hi>; and Raschi, כפה <hi type="italic">inclinavit s. subegit me</hi>. Luther follows these in his rendering, "He rolls me in the ashes," which is a figure signifying the deepest disgrace and humiliation, or a hyperbolical expression for sprinkling with ashes (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.30">Eze 27:30</reference>), as a token of descent into the depths of sorrow.
entries.6e7173e723583a6bbc7a8e9fad9663796fd1e2d7: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.17-Lam.3.18">Lam 3:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen14685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14686" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Lam.3.17">Lam 3:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lam.3.18">Lam 3:18</reference> the speaker, in his lamentation, gives expression to that disposition of his heart which has been produced by the misery that has befallen him to so fearful an extent. He has quite given up hopes of attaining safety and prosperity, and his hope in the Lord is gone. In <reference osisRef="Lam.3.17">Lam 3:17</reference> it is a question whether תּזנח is second or third pers. of the imperf. Following the lxx, who give the rendering ἀπώσατο ἐξ εἰρήνης ψυχήν μου, Rosenmüller, Gesenius, De Wette, and Nägelsbach consider זנח transitive, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.2.7">Deu 2:7</reference>, and take תּזנח as of the second pers.: "Thou didst reject my soul (me) from peace." But to this view of the words there is the decided objection, that neither before nor after is there any direct address to Jahveh, and that the verbs which immediately follow stand in the first person, and succeed the first clause appropriately enough, provided we take נפשׁי as the subject to תּזנח (third pers.). זנח has both a transitive and an intransitive meaning in Kal; cf. Hos 8:3 (trans.) and Hos 8:5 (intrans.). Nägelsbach has no ground for casting doubt on the intrans. meaning in Hos 8:5. Moreover, the objection that the passage now before us is a quotation from <reference osisRef="Ps.88.15">Psa 88:15</reference> (Nägelsbach) does not prove that תּזנח נפשׁי is to be taken in the same sense here as in that passage: "O Jahveh, Thou despisest my soul." By adding משּׁלום, Jeremiah has made an independent reproduction of that passage in the Psalms, if he had it before his mind. This addition does not permit of our attaching a transitive sense to תּזנח, for the verb means to despise, not to reject; hence we cannot render the words, "Thou didst reject my soul from peace." The meaning of the clause is not "my soul loathes prosperity," as it is rendered by Thenius, who further gives the sense as follows: "I had such a thorough disgust for life, that I had no longer the least desire for prosperity." As Gerlach has already remarked, this explanation neither harmonizes with the meaning of שׁלום, not with the expression of doubt in the following verse, which implies a very lively "sense of the prosperous;" moreover, it has no good lexical basis. The fundamental meaning of זנח is to stink, be rancid, from which comes the metaphorical one of instilling disgust, - <hi type="italic">not</hi>, feeling disgust (Hos 8:5), - and further, that of despising. The meaning "to instil disgust" does not suit this passage, but only that of being despised. "My soul is despised of prosperity," i.e., so that it shares not in prosperity; with this accords the intransitive use of the Hiphil הזניח with מן, 2Ch 11:14. The Vulgate, which does not catch the idea of זנח so exactly, renders the passage by <hi type="italic">expulsa est a pace anima mea</hi>. To this there are appropriately joined the words, "I have forgotten good" (good fortune), because I constantly experience nothing but misfortune; and not less appropriate is the expression of doubt, "I say (i.e., I think) my strength and my hope from Jahveh is gone (vanished)," i.e., my strength is worn out through suffering, and I have nothing more to hope for from Jahveh. Starting from the fundamental idea of stability, permanence, נצח, according to the traditional explanation, means vigor, strength; then, by a metaphor, <hi type="italic">vis vitalis</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.3">Isa 63:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.6">Isa 63:6</reference>, - <hi type="italic">not</hi> trust (Rosenmüller, Thenius, Nägelsbach, etc.), in support of which we are pointed to <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.29">1Sa 15:29</reference>, but without sufficient reason; see Delitzsch on Isaiah, <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi> The complaint here attains its deepest and worst. The complainant in his thoughts has gone far from God, and is on the very verge of despair. But here also begins the turning-point. When for the first time he utters the name of God in the expression "my hope from Jahveh," he shows that Jahveh is to him also still the ground of hope and trust. Hence also he not merely complains, "my strength is gone," etc., but introduces this thought with the words ואמר, "I said," sc. in my heart, i.e., I thought, "my strength is gone, and my hope from Jahveh lost," i.e., vanished. The mention of the name <hi type="italic">Jahveh</hi>, i.e., the Covenant-God, keeps him from sinking into despair, and urges him not to let go his trust on the Lord, so that he can now (in what follows) complain to the Lord of his state of distress, and beseech His help.
entries.a348d1ec6c327c81aca7f8ccde3d66c0527c5939: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.19">Lam 3:19</reference> <div eID="gen14686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14687" type="x-p"/> Consideration of God’s compassion and His omnipotence as displayed at critical junctures in the affairs of men. C. B. Michaelis has correctly perceived, and thus set forth, the transition from the complaint, bordering on despair, to hope, as given in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.19">Lam 3:19</reference> : <hi type="italic">luctatur hic contra desperationis adfectum, quo tentatus fuerat</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.18">Lam 3:18</reference>, <hi type="italic">mix inde per fidem emersurus</hi>. In like manner it is said in the <hi type="italic">Berleburger Bibel</hi>, "In <reference osisRef="Lam.3.19">Lam 3:19</reference> he struggles with despair, to which he had been tempted, and in the following verse soars up once more into the region of faith." By the resumption of עני from <reference osisRef="Lam.3.1">Lam 3:1</reference>, and of לענה and ראשׁ from <reference osisRef="Lam.3.15">Lam 3:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lam.3.5">Lam 3:5</reference>, the contents of the whole preceding lamentation are given in a summary, and by זכר are presented to God in prayer. "Mine affliction" is intensified by the addition of "my persecution" (see on <reference osisRef="Lam.1.7">Lam 1:7</reference>), and the contents of the lamentation thereby more plainly pointed out. This connection of the verse has been misunderstood in many ways. An old interpretation of the words, still maintained by Böttcher and Thenius, makes זכר an infinitive; according to this view, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.19">Lam 3:19</reference> would require to be conjoined with the preceding, and the inf. without ל would stand for the ground, <hi type="italic">recordando</hi>, "while I think of," - which is grammatically impossible.<note placement="foot">Seb. Münster long since said: <hi type="italic">Secundum quosdam est</hi> זכר <hi type="italic">infinit., ut sit sensus: periit spes mea, recordante me afflictionis meae</hi>. Calvin also gives the preference to this view, with the remark: <hi type="italic">Videtur enim hic propheta exprimere, quomodo fere a spe exciderit, ut nihil reperiret amplius fortitudinis in Deo, quia scilicet oppressus erat malis;</hi> in support of which he affirms that it is<hi type="italic">valde absurdum, eos qui experti sunt aliquando Dei misericordiam, sic omnem spem abjicere, ut non statuant amplius sibi esse refugium ad Deum</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen14687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14688" type="x-p"/> The same remark applies to the assumption that זכר is an infinitive which is resumed in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.20">Lam 3:20</reference> : "it thinks of my misery...yes, my soul thinks thereon" (Böttcher, Thenius). Gerlach very properly remarks concerning this view that such a construction is unexampled, and, as regards the change in the form of the infinitive (constr. and abs.), would be unintelligible. The objection of Thenius, however, that the imperative meaning usually attached to זכר is against the whole context, and quite inappropriate here, is connected with the erroneous assumption that <reference osisRef="Lam.3.19">Lam 3:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lam.3.20">Lam 3:20</reference> form a continuation of what precedes, and that the idea of the speaker’s being completely overwhelmed by the thought of all that he had suffered and still suffers, forms the proper conclusion of the first part, after which, from <reference osisRef="Lam.3.21">Lam 3:21</reference> onwards, there follows relief. Gerlach has rightly opposed to these arguments the following considerations: (1) That, after the outburst of despair in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.18">Lam 3:18</reference>, "my strength is gone, and my hope from Jahveh," the words "my soul is bowed down in me" form far too feeble a conclusion; (2) That it is undoubtedly more correct to make the relief begin with a prayer breathed out through sighs (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.19">Lam 3:19</reference>), than with such a reflection as is expressed in Lam 3:21. Ewald also is right in taking זכר as an imperative, but is mistaken in the notion that the speaker addresses any one who is ready to hear him; this view is shown to be erroneous by the simple fact that, in what precedes and succeeds, the thoughts of the speaker are directed to God only.
entries.4b7c91baf052e789f1ca7d4bf2f3d32c4892700b: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.20-Lam.3.23">Lam 3:20-23</reference> <div eID="gen14688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14689" type="x-p"/> The view taken of this verse will depend on the answer to the question whether תּזכר is second or third pers. fem. Following in the wake of Luther ("Thou wilt assuredly think thereon"), C. B. Michaelis, Pareau, Rosenmüller, and Kalkschmidt take it as second pers.: "Think, yea, think wilt Thou, that my soul is bowed down in me," or "that my soul is at rest within me" (Nägelsbach). But it is impossible to maintain either of these views in the face of the language employed. To take the ו before תּשׁיח in the meaning of <hi type="italic">quod</hi> is characterized by Nägelsbach as an arbitrary procedure, unwarranted either by <reference osisRef="Gen.30.27">Gen 30:27</reference> or <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.11">Eze 13:11</reference>; but neither can the meaning of resting, being at east, which is attributed to שׁוּח or שׁיח by that writer, be established. The verb means to sink down, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.18">Pro 2:18</reference>, and metaphorically, to be bowed down, Psa 44:26. The latter meaning is required in the present passage, from the simple fact that the sentence undeniably refers to Psa 42:6.<note placement="foot">Luther’s translation, "for my soul tells me," is founded on the circumstance that the lxx have mistaken שׁיח for שׂיח: καταδολεσχήσει ἐπ ̓ ἐμὲ ἡ ψυχή μου.</note> ותּשׁיח expresses the consequence of זכר תּזכר, which therefore can only be the third pers., and "my soul" the subject of both clauses; for there is no logical consecution of the meaning given by such a rendering as, "If Thou wilt remember, my soul shall be bowed within me." The expression, "If my soul duly meditates thereon (on the deep suffering), it becomes depressed within me," forms the foundation of the request that God would think of his distress, his misery; and <reference osisRef="Lam.3.21">Lam 3:21</reference>, "I will lay this to heart," connects itself with the leading thought set forth in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.19">Lam 3:19</reference>, the reason for which is given in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.20">Lam 3:20</reference>, viz., that my soul is only bowed down within me over the thought of my distress, and must complain of it to God, that He may think of it and alleviate it: This will I lay to heart and set my hope upon. על־כּן is a strong inferential expression: "therefore," because God alone can help, will I hope. This self-encouragement begins with <reference osisRef="Lam.3.22">Lam 3:22</reference>, inasmuch as the prophet strengthens his hope by a consideration of the infinite compassion of the Lord. (It is) חסדי, "the mercies of God," i.e., proofs of His mercy (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.89.2">Psa 89:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.43">Psa 107:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">Isa 63:7</reference>), "that we are not utterly consumed," as Luther and similarly our English translators have excellently rendered תּמנוּ. This form stands for תּמּונוּ, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.44.18">Jer 44:18</reference>; Num 17:1-13 :28, not for תּמּוּ, third pers., as Pareau, Thenius, Vaihinger, and Ewald, referring to his <hi type="italic">Grammar</hi>, §84, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, would take it. The proofs of the grace of God have their foundation in His compassion, from which they flow. In <reference osisRef="Lam.3.23">Lam 3:23</reference> we take חסדי  as the subject of חדשׁים; it is the proofs of the grace of God that are new every morning, not "His compassions," although the idea remains the same. לבּקרים, every morning, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">Isa 33:2</reference>; Psa 73:14. <hi type="italic">Ubi sol et dies oritur, simul et radii hujus inexhaustae bonitatis erumpunt</hi> (Tarnovius in Rosenmüller). The consciousness of this constant renewal of the divine favour impels to the prayerful exclamation, "great is Thy faithfulness;" cf. Psa 36:6.
entries.6025d2495e5330fe2021b72e8dfe22c2ceae98bf: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.24-Lam.3.28">Lam 3:24-28</reference> "My portion is Jahveh:" this is a reminiscence from <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.26">Psa 73:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.6">Psa 142:6</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.57">Psa 119:57</reference>, where the expression found here is repeated almost <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi>. The expression is based on Num 18:20, where the Lord says to Aaron, "I am thy portion and thine inheritance;" i.e., Jahveh will be to the tribe of Levi what the other tribes receive in their territorial possessions in Canaan; Levi shall have his possession and enjoyment in Jahveh. The last clause, "therefore will I hope," etc., is a repetition of what is in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Lam.3.21">Lam 3:21</reference></hi>, as if by way of refrain. <div eID="gen14689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14690" type="x-p"/> This hope cannot be frustrated, Lam 3:25. The fundamental idea of the section contained in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.25-Lam.3.33">Lam 3:25-33</reference> is thus stated by Nägelsbach: "The Lord is well disposed towards the children of men under all circumstances; for even when He smites them, He seeks their highest interest: they ought so to conduct themselves in adversity, that it is possible for Him to carry out His designs." On <reference osisRef="Lam.3.25">Lam 3:25</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.34.9">Psa 34:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.5">Psa 86:5</reference>; and on the general meaning, also <reference osisRef="Ps.25.3">Psa 25:3</reference>; Psa 69:7. If the Lord is kind to those who hope in Him, then it is good for man to wait patiently for His help in suffering. Such is the mode in which <reference osisRef="Lam.3.26">Lam 3:26</reference> is attached to Lam 3:25. טוב, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.26">Lam 3:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lam.3.27">Lam 3:27</reference>, followed by ל <hi type="italic">dat</hi>., means to be good for one, i.e., beneficial. Some expositors (Gesenius, Rosenmüller, Maurer, Nägelsbach) take יחיל as a noun-form, substantive or adjective; דּוּמם is then also taken in the same way, and ו - ו as correlative: "it is good both to wait and be silent." But although there are analogous cases to support the view that יחיל is a noun-form, the constant employment of דּוּמם as an adverb quite prevents us from taking it as an adjective. Moreover, "to be silent for the help of the Lord," would be a strange expression, and we would rather expect "to be silent and wait for;" and finally, waiting and silence are so closely allied, that the disjunctive ו - ו <hi type="italic">et - et</hi> appears remarkable. We prefer, then, with Ewald (<hi type="italic">Gram</hi>. §235, <hi type="italic">a</hi>) and others, to take יחיל as a verbal form, and that, too, in spite of the <hi type="italic">i</hi> in the jussive form of the Hiphil for יחל, from חוּל, in the meaning of יחל, to wait, tarry. "It is good that he (man) should wait, and in silence too (i.e., without complaining), for the help of the Lord." On the thought presented here, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.38.7">Psa 38:7</reference> and Isa 30:15. Hence it is also good for man to bear a yoke in youth (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.27">Lam 3:27</reference>), that he may exercise himself in calm waiting on the help of the Lord. In the present context the yoke is that of sufferings, and the time of youth is mentioned as the time of freshness and vigour, which render the bearing of burdens more easy. He who has learned in youth to bear sufferings, will not sink into despair should they come on him in old age. Instead of בּנעוּריו, Theodotion has ἐκ νεότητος αὐτοῦ, which is also the reading of the Aldine edition of the lxx; and some codices have מנּעוּריו. But this reading is evidently a correction, prompted by the thought that Jeremiah, who composed the Lamentations in his old age, had much suffering to endure from the time of his call to the prophetic office, in the earlier portion of his old age; nor is it much better than the inference of J. D. Michaelis, that Jeremiah composed this poem when a youth, on the occasion of King Josiah’s death. - In <reference osisRef="Lam.3.28-Lam.3.30">Lam 3:28-30</reference>, the effect of experience by suffering is set forth, yet not in such a way that the verses are to be taken as still dependent on כּי in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.27">Lam 3:27</reference> (Luther, Pareau, De Wette, Maurer, and Thenius): "that he should sit alone and be silent," etc. Such a combination is opposed to the independent character of each separate alphabetic strophe. Rather, the result of early experience in suffering and patience is developed in a cohortative form. The connection of thought is simply as follows: Since it is good for man that he should learn to endure suffering, let him sit still and bear it patiently, when God puts such a burden on him. Let him sit solitary, as becomes those in sorrow (see on <reference osisRef="Lam.1.1">Lam 1:1</reference>), and be silent, without murmuring (cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.3.26">Lam 3:26</reference>), when He lays a burden on him. There is no object to נטל expressly mentioned, but it is easily understood from the notion of the verb (if He lays anything on him), or from על in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.27">Lam 3:27</reference> (if He lays a yoke on him). We are forbidden to consider the verbs as indicatives ("he sits alone and is silent;" Gerlach, Nägelsbach) by the apocopated form יתּן in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.29">Lam 3:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.30">Lam 3:30</reference>, which shows that ישׁב and ידּם are also cohortatives.
entries.2c92b4301b5e42d055b962342615ad181c458d4e: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.29">Lam 3:29</reference> "Let him put his mouth in the dust," i.e., humbly bow beneath the mighty hand of God. The expression is derived from the Oriental custom of throwing oneself in the most reverential manner on the ground, and involves the idea of humble silence, because the mouth, placed in the dust, cannot speak. The clause, "perhaps there is hope," indicates the frame of mind to be observed in the submission. While the man is to show such resignation, he is not to give up the hope that God will deliver him from trouble; cf. <reference osisRef="Job.11.18">Job 11:18</reference>; Jer 31:17.
entries.344494d0f2c778aa15a14b4308162167284ceb3b: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.30-Lam.3.36">Lam 3:30-36</reference> <div eID="gen14690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14691" type="x-p"/> Let him also learn patiently to bear abuse and reviling from men. Let him present his cheek to him who smites him, as was done by Job (<reference osisRef="Job.16.10">Job 16:10</reference>) and the servant of Jahveh (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Isa 50:6</reference>); cf. Mat 5:39. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Lam.3.30">Lam 3:30</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.88.4">Psa 88:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.123.3">Psa 123:3</reference>, etc. There is a certain gradation in the three verses that it quite unmistakeable. The sitting alone and in silence is comparatively the easiest; it is harder to place the mouth in the dust, and yet cling to hope; it is most difficult of all to give the cheek to the smiter, and to satiate oneself with dishonour (Nägelsbach). In <reference osisRef="Lam.3.31-Lam.3.33">Lam 3:31-33</reference> follow the grounds of comfort. The first is in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.31">Lam 3:31</reference> : the sorrow will come to an end; the Lord does not cast off for ever; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">Jer 3:5</reference>, Jer 3:12. The second is in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.32">Lam 3:32</reference> : when He has caused sorrow, He shows pity once more, according to the fulness of His grace. Compassion outweighs sorrow. On this subject, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.30.6">Psa 30:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.5.18">Job 5:18</reference>; Isa 54:8. The third ground of comfort is in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.33">Lam 3:33</reference> : God does not send affliction willingly, as if it brought Him joy (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.32.41">Jer 32:41</reference>), but merely because chastisement is necessary to sinful man for the increase of his spiritual prosperity; cf. <reference osisRef="Acts.14.22">Act 14:22</reference>; 2Co 4:17. ויּגּה is for וייגּה: cf. Ewald, §232, <hi type="italic">f</hi>; Gesenius, §69, 3, Rem. 6. <div eID="gen14691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14692" type="x-p"/> That he may bring home to the hearts of God’s people the exhortation to bear suffering with patience and resignation, and that he may lead them to see that the weight of sorrow under which they are sighing has been sent from the Lord as a chastisement for their sins, the prophet carries out the thought, in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.34-Lam.3.39">Lam 3:34-39</reference>, that every wrong committed upon earth is under the divine control (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.34-Lam.3.36">Lam 3:34-36</reference>), and generally that nothing happens without God’s permission; hence man ought not to mourn over the suffering that befalls him, but rather over his sins (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.37-Lam.3.39">Lam 3:37-39</reference>).
entries.21e40064df0cd66fcd788d682b80e2645ba47140: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.37-Lam.3.39">Lam 3:37-39</reference> <div eID="gen14693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14694" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.37">Lam 3:37</reference> brings the answer to this question in a lively manner, and likewise in an interrogative form: "Who hath spoken, and it came to pass, which the Lord hath not commanded?" The thought here presented reminds us of the word of the Creator in Gen 1:3. The form of the expression is an imitation of Psa 33:9. Rosenmüller gives the incorrect rendering, <hi type="italic">Quis est qui dixit: factum est</hi> (i.e., <hi type="italic">quis audeat dicere fieri quicquam), non praecipiente Deo</hi>; although the similar but more free translation of Luther, "Who dares to say that such a thing happens without the command of the Lord?" gives the sense in a general way. The meaning is as follows: Nothing takes place on the earth which the Lord has not appointed; no man can give and execute a command against the will of God. From this it further follows (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.38">Lam 3:38</reference>), that evil and good will proceed from the mouth of the Lord, i.e., be wrought by Him; on this point, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.45.7">Isa 45:7</reference>; Amo 3:6. לא תצא gives no adequate meaning unless it be taken interrogatively, and as indicating what is usual - wont to be. And then there is established from this, in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.39">Lam 3:39</reference>, the application of the general principle to the particular case in question, viz., the grievous suffering of individuals at the downfall of the kingdom of Judah. "Why does a man sigh as long as he lives? Let every one [sigh] for his sins." Man is not to sigh over suffering and sorrow, but only over his sin. התאונן occurs only here and in Num 11:1, and signifies to sigh, with the accessory notion of murmuring, complaining. חי appended to אדם is more of a predicate than a simple attributive: man, as long as he lives, i.e., while he is in this life. The verse is viewed in a different light by Pareau, Ewald, Neumann, and Gerlach, who combine both members into one sentence, and render it thus: "Why doth a man complain, so long as he lives, - a man over the punishment of his sins?" [Similar is the rendering of our "Authorized" Version.] Neumann translates: "A man in the face of [Ger. <hi type="italic">bei</hi>] his sins." But this latter rendering is lexically inadmissible, because על esua in this connection cannot mean "in view of." The other meaning assigned is improbable, though there is nothing against it, lexically considered. For though חטא, sin, may also signify the punishment of sin, the latter meaning does not suit the present context, because in what precedes it is not said that the people suffer for their sins, but merely that their suffering has been appointed by God. If, then, in what follows, there is an exhortation to return to the Lord (Lam 3:40.), and in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.42">Lam 3:42</reference> a confession of sins made; if, moreover, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.39">Lam 3:39</reference> forms the transition from <reference osisRef="Lam.3.33-Lam.3.38">Lam 3:33-38</reference> to the exhortation that succeeds (Lam 3:40.); then it is not abstinence from murmuring or sighing over the punishment of sins that forms the true connecting link of the two lines of thought, but merely the refraining from complaint over sufferings, coupled with the exhortation to sigh over their won sins. Tarnov also has viewed the verse in this way, when he deduces from it the advice to every soul labouring under a weight of sorrows: <hi type="italic">est igitur optimus ex malis emergendi modus Deum excusare et se ipsum accusare</hi>.
entries.16e71b5a944d61a255d78d84abb4c095216c1079: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.40-Lam.3.42">Lam 3:40-42</reference> <div eID="gen14694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14695" type="x-p"/> Confession of sins, and complaint against the cruelty of enemies, as well as over the deep misery into which all the people have sunk. <reference osisRef="Lam.3.40">Lam 3:40</reference>-42. The acknowledgment of guilt implies to prayer, to which also there is a summons in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.40">Lam 3:40</reference>, Lam 3:41. The transitional idea is not, "Instead of grumbling in a sinful spirit, let us rather examine our conduct" (Thenius); for the summons to examine one’s conduct is thereby placed in contrast with <reference osisRef="Lam.3.39">Lam 3:39</reference>, and the thought, "let every one mourn over his own sins," transformed into a prohibition of sinful complaint. The real transition link is given by Rosenmüller: <hi type="italic">quum mala nostra a peccatis nostris oriantur, culpas nostras et scrutemur et corrigamus</hi>. The searching of our ways, i.e., of our conduct, if it be entered on in an earnest spirit, must end in a return to the Lord, from whom we have departed. It is self-evident that עד יהוה does not stand for אל יי, but means as far as (even to) Jahveh, and indicates thorough conversion - no standing half-way. The lifting up of the heart to the hands, also, - not merely of the hands to God, - expresses earnest prayer, that comes from the heart. אל־כּפּים, to the hands (that are raised towards heaven). "To God in heaven," where His almighty throne is placed (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Psa 2:4</reference>), that He may look down from thence (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.59">Lam 3:59</reference>) and send help. With <reference osisRef="Lam.3.42">Lam 3:42</reference> begins the prayer, as is shown by the direct address to God in the second member. There is no need, however, on this account, for supplying לאמר before the first member; the command to pray is immediately followed by prayer, beginning with the confession of sins, and the recognition of God’s chastisement; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.106.6">Psa 106:6</reference>; Dan 9:5. נחנוּ is contrasted with אתּה. "Thou hast not pardoned," because Thy justice must inflict punishment.
entries.67f5a06a9f2b5be13b8cbcf082a7f07d39e239d0: <reference osisRef="Lam.3.43-Lam.3.48">Lam 3:43-48</reference> <div eID="gen14695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14696" type="x-p"/> God has not pardoned, but positively punished, the people for their misdeeds. "Thou hast covered with anger," <reference osisRef="Lam.3.43">Lam 3:43</reference>, corresponds to "Thou hast covered with a cloud," <reference osisRef="Lam.3.44">Lam 3:44</reference>; hence "Thou hast covered" is plainly used both times in the same meaning, in spite of the fact that לך is wanting in Lam 3:43. סכך means to "cover," here to "make a cover." "Thou didst make a cover with anger," i.e., Thou didst hide Thyself in wrath; there is no necessity for taking סכך as in itself reflexive. This mode of viewing it agrees also with what follows. The objection of J. D.
