Though, then, human reason may say, that God does not see, but neglect and disregard his people, yet on the other hand, this doctrine ought to sustain them, it being certain that God does see them. This is the reason why David so often uses this mode of expression.
Thou, Jehovah, he says, hast seen all their vengeances By vengeances here he means acts of violence, according to what we find in Psalm 8:2, where God is said “to put to flight the enemy and the avenger.” By the avenger there he simply means, not such as retaliate wrongs, but cruel and violent men. So also, in this place, by vengeances, he means all kinds of cruelty, as also by thoughts he means wicked counsels, by which the ungodly sought to oppress the miserable and the innocent. He again repeats the same thing, —
Lamentations 3:61
61. Thou hast heard their reproach, O LORD, and all their imaginations against me;
61. Audivisti probra ipsorum, Jehova, omnes cogitationes eorum contra me.
entries.f0a69ad5a206038f9ffefd5a1d838d222765ab16:
We see that this is a repetition, but for vengeances he now mentions reproaches And in this way he sought again to turn God to mercy; for when he brings no aid, he seems to close his eyes and to render his ears deaf; but when he attends to our evils, he then soon brings help. The Prophet, then, having said that God saw, now refers to hearing: he had heard their reproaches. Adopting a language not strictly proper, he adds, that he had heard their thoughts; though he speaks not only of their secret counsels, but also of all the wicked conspiracies by which his enemies had contrived to ruin him.
There is no necessity, as some have supposed, of making לי in the former verse, and עלי in this verse, the same. The difference is occasioned by the verbs “thou hast seen,” and, “thou hast heard.” God had seen the thoughts or purposes effected “against” him; and he had heard the purposes formed “concerning” him. He refers first to the purposes carried into effect, and then, as it is common in the prophets, he refers to the purposes previously formed respecting him. — Ed
He adds, —
Lamentations 3:62
62. The lips of those that rose up against me, and their device against me all the day.
62. Labia (vel sermones, aut, linguas) insurgebtium contra me, et sermones eorum contra me tota die (vel, quotidie.)
entries.a395c39af40579d1706c4c260c5e1a3c7fd88301:
Instead of thoughts, he now mentions lips, or words. The verb הגה, ege means to meditate, when no voice is uttered; but as the noun is connected here with lips, there is no doubt but that the Prophet refers to words, rather than to hidden meditations.
The best word is muttering, —
The lips of my adversaries, And their muttering concerning me all the day.
It isn’t here, as in the previous verse, “concerning me,” not “against me.” — Ed.
He then says, that such were the conspiracies, that they did not conceal what they had in their hearts, but publicly avowed their wicked purposes. Now this insolence must have moved God to aid his people, so unjustly oppressed.
He adds, every day, or daily. This circumstance also must have availed to obtain favor, so that God might the sooner aid his people. For had the ungodly made violent assaults, and soon given over, it would have been easy to persevere in so short a trial, as when a storm soon passes by; but when they went on perseveringly in their machinations, it was very hard to bear the trial. And hence we derive a ground of hope, supplied to us by what the Holy Spirit suggests to us here, that God will be merciful to us on seeing the pertinacity of our enemies. He then adds, —
Lamentations 3:63
63. Behold their sitting down, and their rising up; I am their musick.
63. Sessionem eorum et surrectionem eorum aspice; ego canticum eorum (vel, pulsatio, ut alii vertunt
entries.37dcc53457552883173f87e4b46a989207163dbe:
The Prophet repeats still the same thing, only in other words. He had spoken of the lyings in wait, and the conspiracies and the speeches of his enemies; he now adds, that nothing was hid from God. By sitting and rising, he means all the actions of life, as when David says,
“Thou knowest my sitting and my rising,” (Psalm 139:2;)
that is, whether I rest or walk, all my actions are known to thee. By rising, then, the Prophet denotes here, as David did, all the movements or doings of men; and by sitting, he means their quiet counsels; for men either deliberate and prepare for work while they sit, or rise, and thus move and act.
He means, in short, that whether his enemies consulted silently and quietly, or attempted to do this or that, nothing was unknown to God. Now, as God takes such notice of the counsels and all the actions of men, it cannot be but that he restrains and checks the wicked; for God’s knowledge is always connected with his office as a judge. We hence see how the Prophet strengthens himself, as we have lately stated, and thus gathers a reason for confidence; for the wicked counsels of his enemies and their works were not hid from God.
He adds, I am become a song He again sets before God his reproach, east upon him by the ungodly. For that indignity also availed much to lead God not to suffer his people to be unworthily treated. It now follows, —
Lamentations 3:64
64. Render unto them a recompence, O LORD, according to the work of their hands.
64. Repende illis mercedem, Jehova, secundum opus manuum suarum
entries.ed8af4e6365488c6421c9f5efa3f832a3feb762f:
He adds here a conclusion; for he has hitherto been relating, as I have said, the evils which he suffered, and also the reproaches and unjust oppressions, in order that; he might have God propitious to him; for this is the way of conciliating favor when we are wrongfully dealt with; for it cannot be but that God will sustain our cause. He indeed testifies that he is ready to help the miserable; it is his own peculiar work to deliver captives from prison, to illuminate the blind, to succor the miserable and the oppressed. This is the reason, then, why the Prophet now confidently asks God to render to his enemies their reward, according to the work of their hands
Were any one to object, and say, that another rule is prescribed to us, even to pray for our enemies, even when they oppress us; the answer is this, that the faithful, when they prayed thus, did not bring any violent feelings of their own, but pure zeal, and rightly formed; for the Prophet here did not pray for evil indiscriminately on all, but on the reprobate, who were perpetually the enemies of God and of his Church. He might then with sincerity of heart have asked God to render to them their just reward. And whenever the saints broke forth thus against their enemies, and asked God to become an avenger, this principle must be ever borne in mind, that they did not indulge their own wishes, but were so guided by the Holy Spirit — that moderation was connected with that fervid zeal to which I have referred. The Prophet, then, as he speaks here of the Chaldeans, confidently asked God to destroy them, as we shall again presently see. We find also in the Psalms the same imprecations, especially on Babylon, — “Happy he who shall render to thee what thou hast brought on us, who shall dash thy children against a stone.” (Psalm 137:8, 9.) It follows, —
Lamentations 3:65
65. Give them sorrow of heart, thy curse unto them.
65. Des illis impedimentum cordis (alii, obstinationem,) maledictionem tuam illis (vel maledictio tua illis.)
entries.34355a5f73103b70f124b06da7cd2a020d89b316:
He expresses what the vengeance was to be, even that God would give them up to a reprobate mind; for by מגנת-לב, meganet-leb, he no doubt meant the blindness of the heart, and at the same time included stupidity, as though he had said, “O Lord, so oppress them with evils, that they may become stupified.” For it is an extremity of evil, when we are so overpowered as not to be as it were ourselves, and when our evils do not drive us to prayer.
The word meant “covering, as rendered by the Sept.; the Syr. Has “sorrow,” and the Vulg. “shield,” which has no meaning. What is no doubt meant is hardness or blindness —
Give them blindness of heart: Thy curse be to them.
— Ed
We now then perceive what the Prophet meant by asking God to give to his enemies the impediment of heart, even that he might take away a sound mind, and smite them with blindness and madness, as it is said elsewhere. — I run on quickly, that I may finish, lest the hour should prevent us. The last verse of this triple alphabet follows, —
Lamentations 3:66
66. Persecute and destroy them in anger from under the heavens of the LORD.
66. Persequere in ira et perde eos e sub coelis Jehovae (quidam in vocativo casu legunt, Jehova; sed quia non ponitur שמים, sed in constructione שמי, ideo retineo proprietatem.)
entries.a1ce1d1df8330b1daef3b50fe98e9cfa9326b7fe:
He first asks God to persecute them in wrath, that is, to be implacable to them; for persecution is, when God not only chastises the wicked for a short time, but when he adds evils to evils, and accumulates them until they perish. He then adds, and prays God to destroy them from under the heavens of Jehovah This phrase is emphatical; and they extenuate the weightiness of the sentence, who thus render it, “that God himself would destroy the ungodly from the earth.” For the Prophet does not without a design mention the heavens of Jehovah, as though he had said, that though God is hidden from us while we sojourn in the world, he yet dwells in heaven, for heaven is often called the throne of God, —
“The heaven is my throne.” (Isaiah 66:1.)
“O God, who dwellest in the sanctuary.” (Psalm 22:4; Psalm 77:14.)
By God’s sanctuary is often meant heaven. For this reason, then, the Prophet asked here that the ungodly should be destroyed from under the heaven of Jehovah, that is, that their destruction might testify that he sits in heaven, and is the judge of the world, and that things are not in such a confusion, but that the ungodly must at length render an account before the celestial judge, whom they have yet long neglected. This is the end of the chapter.
PRAYER.
Grant, Almighty God, that as at this day ungodly men and wholly reprobate so arrogantly rise up against thy Church, we may learn to flee to thee, and to hide ourselves under the shadow of thy wings, and fully to hope for thy salvation; and that however disturbed the state of things may be, we may yet never doubt but that thou wilt be propitious to us, since we have so often found thee to be our deliverer; and that we may thus persevere in confidence of thy grace and mercy, and be also roused by this incentive to pray to thee, until having gone through all our miseries, we shall at length enjoy that blessed rest which thou hast promised to us through Christ Jesus our Lord. — Amen.
CHAPTER 4
Lecture Fourteenth
Lamentations 4:1
1. How is the gold become dim! how is the most fine gold changed! the stones of the sanctuary are poured out in the top of every street.
1. Quomodo obscuratum est aurum! Mutatum est aurum bonum! Effusi sunt (vel, projecti) lapides sanctuarii in capite omnium platearum.

entries.d08501379614260194ec3af01970bbad8e9b0211:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="3" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. III.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 I <ns0:hi>Am</ns0:hi> the man <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Some understand this of the Prophet, some of the People, who were before set out under the Notion of a Woman, a Daughter, here <ns0:hi>of a man.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Affliction must here be taken <ns0:hi>Em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phatically</ns0:hi> for eminent degrees of affliction, caused not meerly from the power and malice of the Enemy, but from the wrath of God, though brought upon them by the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> who were to the two Tribes, the Rod of Gods wrath, as the <ns0:hi>Assyrians</ns0:hi> are called with reference to the ten Tribes, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 10.5.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:70" />2 He hath led me, and brought <ns0:hi>me into</ns0:hi> darkness, but not <ns0:hi>into</ns0:hi> light.<ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Darkness</ns0:hi> in Scripture (metaphorically taken) signifies <ns0:hi>Igno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rance, Sin</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Misery</ns0:hi>; and <ns0:hi>Light</ns0:hi> signifies <ns0:hi>Knowledge,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>state of Grace,</ns0:hi> or a state of <ns0:hi>mirth</ns0:hi> and jollity, they are both here taken in the latter sense, as light is taken, <ns0:hi>Esther</ns0:hi> 8.16. <ns0:hi>Micah.</ns0:hi> 7.8. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 18.5. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 97.11. and also Darkness is used, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 13.16. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 22.29. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 20.19. <ns0:hi>Ioel</ns0:hi> 2.2. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 32.8. the sense is God hath not brought me into a joyful and prospe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rous, but into a sad and calamitous estate and condition.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Surely against me is he turned, he turneth his hand <ns0:hi>against me</ns0:hi> all the day <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The course of Gods Providence toward me is quite altered, his hand, that is his power was wont to be with me and for me against my Enemies, is now turned against me, nor is it for a moment, or for one stroke or two, but his hand is continually against me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 My flesh and my skin hath he made old, he hath broken my bones <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">I was a <ns0:hi>Virgin,</ns0:hi> young and fair, but I am quite altered, and am now as an old woman whose flesh is decayed, and my skin wrinkled; all my beauty is gone, and all my strength is gone, my <ns0:hi>bones,</ns0:hi> those in whom my strength consisted are slain and broken.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 He hath builded against me <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He hath not builded with me increasing my prosperity, and protecting my houses, but he hath builded Forts and Bat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teries and Castles, (military buildings) to batter down my Walls and Houses, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 29.2, 3.</ns0:note>, and compassed me with gall and travel <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or with Poison, Venom and Misery (as some translate it) and it seems more proper than <ns0:hi>gall</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>travel,</ns0:hi> which have no cognation one with another. We are not well acquainted with the ancient Dialect of other Countries, the sense is obvious, God had surrounded them with misery and Calamities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 5, 6.</ns0:note> He hath set me in dark places, as <ns0:hi>they that be</ns0:hi> dead of old <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Prophet compareth their state in <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> to the state of bodies in the Graves, or in some <ns0:hi>Charnel</ns0:hi> house, which are places of darkness, full of rottenness and dead mens bones. Such was the state of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> during the time of the siege before the City was taken, when <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> was a most miserable place by reason of the multitudes slain by the Enemy, or by the Famine: such was their estate in <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> where the company of Heathens made their state, as the state of the living amongst the dead.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 3.23. & 19.8.</ns0:note> He hath hedged me about, that I cannot get out <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The use of an hedge about an inclosed field, is twofold: To keep out other beasts, which belong not to the owner of the ground; in this sense God set an hedge sometimes about <ns0:hi>Cana<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />an, Isa.</ns0:hi> 5.5. 2 To keep in those beasts that are within, thus God had now hedged them in, into a barren place where they had no pasture, but were continually pushed at by other beasts with whom they were mixed, and who were stronger than they, and they could not get out.</ns0:note>: he hath made my chain heavy <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">God had dealt with them as with grievous Malefactors, who are loaded with heavy Chains. He had made their affliction heavy and insupportable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Also when I cry and shout <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">In the condition I am in, I cannot help my self, no crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures can help me, I have no hope but in God, I take the or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary course in that case, which is prayer, I pray fervently and aloud, as those that are serious and importunate for what they de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sire (for shouting here signifies no more than making a loud noise, not a loud noise of Joy and rejoycing, as it mostly signifies) but he deals with me as great persons that have no mind to listen to Suitors, and shut their gates against them, he shutteth out my supplications, which made their case wholly desperate and remediless.</ns0:note>, he shutteth out my prayer <ns0:hi>m.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 He hath inclosed my wayes with hewen stones <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Wayes</ns0:hi> in Scripture ordinarily signifies mens Courses, and methods of Counsels, and actions if the term be taken in that sense here, it signifieth Gods defeating all their methods and counsels taken for their own security in the pursuit of which they met not with ordinary, but with insuperable difficulties like Walls of hewen stone.</ns0:note>, he hath made my pathes crooked <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Nay God had not onely defeated their Counsels, but had made them prove fatal and pernicious to themselves, which seemeth to be intended, by making their wayes crooked, which should have led right on to the end intended.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job. 10.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Isa 38.13. Hos. 5.14. & 17.7, 8.</ns0:note> He <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> unto me <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> a bear lying in wait, <ns0:hi>and as</ns0:hi> a lion in secret places <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That is, he hath taken all advantages against me to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroy me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 He hath turned aside my wayes, and pulled me in pieces, he hath made me desolate <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The same thing is repeated in other Phrases, which was before said, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> That God had pleased by his Providence to frustrate all the designs and counsels of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and miserably to destroy them, as a Lion, or a Bear (the wild beasts menti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />oned before) tear in pieces the Beasts they prey upon.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 He hath bent his bow, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 7.2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 16.12.</ns0:note> set me as a mark for the arrow <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">He hath prepared himself for acts of vindicative Justice, and he hath made me the object of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 He hath caused the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> arrows of his qui<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver to enter into my reins <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">That is, he hath made his judgments, to pierce the most inward parts of the nation; or he hath mortally wounded me. In the <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> it is the <ns0:hi>daughters of his quiver,</ns0:hi> a way of speaking very usual in <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> to express any thing that comes from another as the effect either of a natural or moral cause, so sparks are called the <ns0:hi>Sons of the quick coal, Iob</ns0:hi> 5.7. and corn the <ns0:hi>Son of the floor.</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 I was <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 20.7.</ns0:note> a derision to all my people, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 30.9 Psal. 69.12. Ver. 63.</ns0:note> their song all the day <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Though some think the Prophet speakes this of himself, yet, considering he hath all along spoken in the name of the people it is not probable, which makes a difficulty, how the people could be a derision to themselves? It seemeth therefore ill translated, and that it should have been, <ns0:hi>I was a derision to all people,</ns0:hi> leaving out <ns0:hi>my,</ns0:hi> that is, to all forreigners, to whom the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were made a derision and an hissing, there onely wants the last letter in <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and it is well observed by the learned Authour of the <ns0:hi>English Annotations</ns0:hi> that the like defect is to be found as to the same word, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 24.43. compared with <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 18.43. so that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> is not a <ns0:hi>Pronoun affix</ns0:hi> (upon which sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posal our Translators go) but one of the Letters that form the plural number, the other being left out, and <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> put for <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 He hath filled me with <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>bit<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nesses.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">That is, he hath filled me with severe and bitter dispensa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions, wormwood is a bitter herb, but it is also a wholesome herb, and therefore some think that the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word should rather be translated <ns0:hi>Henbane,</ns0:hi> and that it signifies some herb whose juice is intoxicating and poisonous.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 He hath also broken my teeth with gravel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stones, he hath <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>rolled <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> in the ashes.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> covered me with ashes <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">These are but more metaphorical expressions signifying the unpleasant difficult condition into which God had brought this people. They were like men that lived upon gritty bread, more fit to break their teeth than to nourish them, they were in the state of Mourners, and no ordinary Mourners, who were wont to throw ashes on their heads, they were all over covered with ashes.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And thou hast removed my soul far off from peace <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Peace,</ns0:hi> here signifieth <ns0:hi>prosperity,</ns0:hi> rather than a <ns0:hi>freedom from war.</ns0:hi> Though during the siege they were far from peace in a strict sense, yet in their captivity they had that peace, but both their minds were far off from quiet, and their persons from pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sperity, the Prophet owneth God as the cause of this.</ns0:note>: I forgat <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> prosperity <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">They had in <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> lived prosperously, but now they thought of it no more, nor understood what such a thing meant.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 And I said, My strength and my hope is perished from the LORD.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> Remembring mine affliction and my mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sery, the wormwood and the gall <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">If according to our translation we read <ns0:hi>Remembring,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>while I remember,</ns0:hi> these two verses contain but one sentence; in the former part the Prophet in the name of this People expres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seth their despairing condition; in the latter he gives the reason of it. <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the Peoples poring upon their great, and heavy afflictions, which he compares to <ns0:hi>wormwood</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>gall,</ns0:hi> two things excessively bitter, and often made use of to signifie great affli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 69.21. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> .8.14. and 9.15. and 23.15. <ns0:hi>R<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>v.</ns0:hi> 8.11. But it may as well be read <ns0:hi>imperatively, Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />member</ns0:hi> mine affliction, so the first of these two verses expresseth the dejection of the Peoples minds in their Cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tivity caused through their proneness to despair of any better condition that their angry God would bring them into. The 29th. <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> is a prayer directed to God, which shewed that though they were mightily perplexed, yet they were not in utter despair; and to this sense the following verses seem to incline.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:70" />20 My soul hath <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> still in remembrance: and is <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>Bowed.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> humbled within me <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">That is, I cannot forget them, and the thoughts of them sink my spirits.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 This I <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>I make to return to my <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>art.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> recall to my mind, therefore have I hope <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>This,</ns0:hi> not what was already said, that made them despair, and their souls to bow down; but <ns0:hi>this,</ns0:hi> that which followeth, concerning the Nature of God, and other good Providences. I see nothing in the circumstances of my condition to comfort me, but I see somthing in Gods Nature, and in some other dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pensations of his Providence, which gives me ground to hope for better things than an utter ruine and destruction.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 ¶ <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mal. 3.6.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>It is of</ns0:hi> the LORDs mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Mercy is nothing else but love flowing freely from any, to persons in misery, and differs from compassion onely in the free<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of the emanation. It is not because God had not power enough utterly to have consumed us, nor because we had not guilt enough to have provoked his Justice to have put an end to our lives, as well as to the lives of many thousands of our Countrymen, but it is meerly from the Lords free love and pity to us in our miseries. If God had not a blessing in store for us, how is it that we are captives and not slain as many o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers were during the siege?</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:hi>They are</ns0:hi> new every morning, great <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy faithfulness <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">These compassions of God are renewed day by day, to declare the great faithfulness of God in fulfilling his many pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mises ma<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> for Mercy to his people.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 The LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 16.5. & 73: 26. & 119.57. Jer. 10.16.</ns0:note> portion, saith my soul, therefore will I hope in him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">God is the portion of his People, and they have chosen him as their portion, he hath declared himself to them as such, and they have accepted him as such. This gives them ground both for Patience under his Providences, and also of expecta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of good from him in their lowest and meanest state.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 The LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> good to them that wait for him, to the soul <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> seeketh him <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Good is a term of a very comprehensive notion. The na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture of it lieth in a sutableness to the thing or person to whom it relateth. So it signifieth <ns0:hi>profit</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>pleasantness.</ns0:hi> There is in God an essential goodness, which is his absolute perfection; but this Text speaketh of a communicative goodness, which floweth from him to his Creatures, and is seen in his suting their various necessities and desires with satisfactory dispensa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions of Providence. Though God be in one degree or other good to all, yet he is more especially good to the true wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shippers of him, yet possibly not in their seasons or times when they expect or would have God shew himself so to them, in this or that way, but alwayes to those who wait for him, pati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ently induring trials and afflictions until God please to send them deliverance.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> good that <ns0:hi>a man</ns0:hi> should both hope, and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Good here either signifies <ns0:hi>honestum,</ns0:hi> what becomes men, and is their duty; or <ns0:hi>Vtile,</ns0:hi> what is profitable, and will turn to good account to them. <ns0:hi>Hoping</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>waiting</ns0:hi> differ but as the <ns0:hi>mother</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>daughter.</ns0:hi> Hope being the Mother of Patience and Wait<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, or as the <ns0:hi>Habit</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> Hoping and Waiting being much the same, flowing from a gracious power and habit given the Soul to wait. <ns0:hi>Quietness</ns0:hi> is necessary to <ns0:hi>waiting,</ns0:hi> for all tur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bulen<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>y and impatience of Spirit under sad Providences is op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed to waiting. The Salvation of the Lord refers to the out<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward man, in preserving or delivering us from dangers. Or to the Soul and inward man, in preserving us from, and deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vering our souls out of dangers they fear, or evils they are pressed with. Now for a man in the midst of all evils to hope in God, and without turbulence or disorder in himself, to wait for a preservation from, or a delivery out of any evils is what becometh a man (a child of God especially) and will turn to a good account to them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Good here must be expounded in the same sense as in the foregoing verse. It is not pleasant, but it is profitable, it is honourable, what becomes us, and is our duty, quietly and patiently to bear what afflictions God will please to lay upon us, to restrain our wild and wanton spirits when they are most prone to be too brisk and lascivious. Some by <ns0:hi>yoke</ns0:hi> understand the Law of God, called a yoke (because indeed it is so to flesh and blood) <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11.29. It is not so easie to bend a neck stiffened with Age, or change an heart made hard by Custom. <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> bids us to train up one in their youth in the way we would have them to walk; and whether God will tame us when young, by his Word or by his Rod, it is of advantage to a man: It is also laudable, and what becomes a man, early to bear the yoke of Gods Law, or to bear afflictive Providences, to have his heart betimes humbled to the Will and feet of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 He sitteth alone and keepeth silence, because he hath born <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> upon him <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Our <ns0:hi>English</ns0:hi> Annotations supplying <ns0:hi>That,</ns0:hi> makes the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nexion clear, It is good for a man, that he <ns0:hi>sit alone, Ier.</ns0:hi> 15.17. not doing what he doth to be seen of men, but sitting alone, and when he is alone, suppressing the mutinies of his Spirit and keeping his soul in subjection to God, because God hath hum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bled him by his Rod, humbling himself to his Will.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 He putteth his mouth in the dust, if so be there may be hope <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">If <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> may be supplied, or <ns0:hi>when</ns0:hi> (as <ns0:hi>Pagnine</ns0:hi> translateth <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 28. the connexion of these words with the former is very fair and easie, for then those words, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 27. <ns0:hi>It is good that</ns0:hi> must be repeated in the beginning of <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 28. and 29. how<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever both th s and the former Verses let us know the duty of persons under afflictions in order to their obtaining Mercy at the hand of God, and admirably give us the Character of Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons under afflictions preparing for Mercy. They <ns0:hi>hope,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>quietly wait for Gods Salvation, ver.</ns0:hi> 26. <ns0:hi>they bear Gods yoke, ver.</ns0:hi> 27. because he hath laid it upon them. <ns0:hi>They sit alone and keep silence, ver.</ns0:hi> 28. and here they put <ns0:hi>their mouthes in the dust,</ns0:hi> that is, humble themselves to the feet of God, and to the Will of God; not being too confident of deliverances in this life, but if peradventure <ns0:hi>there may be hope.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 He giveth <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> cheek to him that smiteth him <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">According to our Saviours precept, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.39, he doth not take any private Revenge, he is reproached and reviled, but when he is so he <ns0:hi>revileth not again,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.23. he is fil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led with reproach from others, but his mouth is not filled with the reproachings of others.</ns0:note>: he is filled full with reproach.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 For the LORD will not cast off for ever <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This is that which beareth up his spirits, that though the Lord may for a time estrange himself from his people, yet he will not alwayes forsake them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">But though as a prudent Parent he may see reason to cause grief in, and to afflict his own people, yet as a tender good Father, that pitieth his children in Misery he will have com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />passion upon them, having not onely mercies, but a multitude or abundance of Mercies.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 33.11.</ns0:note> he doth not afflict <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>from his heart.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> willingly, nor grieve the children of men <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">In the Hebrew it is he doth not afflict <ns0:hi>from his heart,</ns0:hi> that is with pleasure and delight; or (which seemeth the best sense to me) not from his own meer motion without a cause given him from the persons afflicted. Hence Judgment is called Gods <ns0:hi>strange work</ns0:hi>; shewing Mercy is his proper natural work, which floweth from himself without any cause in the Creature. Judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment is his <ns0:hi>strange work</ns0:hi> to which he never proceedeth but when provoked, and as it were forced from the Creature, whence it followeth that he cannot delight in it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Here are three things mentioned, of all which it is said, that God approveth them not, neither all, nor any of them. The first is to <ns0:hi>crush the prisoners of the earth,</ns0:hi> he hath power to crush all men in the world, they are his prisoners, and cannot fly from him, but he delighteth not in it, some think it spoken with special reference to the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> who now were all Captives.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 To turn away the right of a man before the face of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>a superiour<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> the most High <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">A second thing which it is said God approveth not, is <ns0:hi>turning away the right of a man before the face of the most high.</ns0:hi> Some, by the most high understand <ns0:hi>God,</ns0:hi> and make the sense to be <ns0:hi>in the sight of God.</ns0:hi> Others think that a Superiour Magistrate is un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood, who <ns0:hi>Eccl.</ns0:hi> 5.8. is called <ns0:hi>the Highest</ns0:hi>; and that seem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the most probable sense. The turning away the right of a man before them, signifieth the use of any arts to deprive them of their just right by misrepresenting their cause aspersing their Persons, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:71" />36 To subvert a man in his cause, the LORD <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>seeth not.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> approveth not <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The third thing mentioned is the <ns0:hi>subverting a man in his cause,</ns0:hi> either by art, and Rhetorick, making it to ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pear bad when it is not so, or by meer Will and Power over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ruling it contrary to right and justice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 ¶ Who is he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 33.9.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> saith, and it com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth to pass, <ns0:hi>when</ns0:hi> the LORD commandeth <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> not <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The sense of these words is doubted by none. That no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing cometh to pass in the World, but by the disposal of Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Providence either effecting it by an immediate influence, but to what end these words are brought in this place is not so generally agreed. Some think they are brought in to check the Blasphemy of some that spake of what had befallen the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> as a thing which God had no hand in. Others think they are brought in as expounding that term that went before, <ns0:hi>The Lord seeth not.</ns0:hi> Though God doth not approve of sinful actions, nor incline any mans Heart or Will to them, yet God hath an hand in the permission of the most cruel and unjust actions, which he could easily hinder. I should rather incline to inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pret them as an argument brought by the Prophet in the name of the People of God, arguing themselves into a quiet submis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion to the afflictive Providences under which they laboured from the consideration of the Superior hand of God in them, as Christ told <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> Thou couldst not have had any power a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst me, if it had not been given thee from above: <ns0:hi>Shall there be evil in a city, and the Lord hath not done it, Amos</ns0:hi> 3.6.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 Out of the mouth of the most High pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceedeth not <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 45.7.</ns0:note> evil and good <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">In the <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the form of these words is interrogatory, as much as if he should say doth not evil come out of Gods mouth from his direction and command, and from his Providence, as well as good? He speaks of evils of punishment, judicial affli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctive dispensations; so it agreeth with <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 2.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 3.6. It is no reproach unto God to make him the Author of his own punishments, though we call them evil.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 19.3.</ns0:note> Wherefore doth a living man <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>murmur.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plain <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This verse admits of various senses, caused from the various interpretation of the Hebrew word which we translate <ns0:hi>complain,</ns0:hi> which also signifies to mourn or grieve, so some render it; why doth a living man grieve or vex himself? but the word is noted most generally to signifie <ns0:hi>complaining</ns0:hi> or murmuring.</ns0:note>? a man for the punishment of his sins <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">The word also which we translate <ns0:hi>Sin,</ns0:hi> sometimes signifieth that oblique act which we call sin; and those who interpret the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer word <ns0:hi>grieve</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>vex,</ns0:hi> thus understand the word translated <ns0:hi>sin,</ns0:hi> supplying some such words as these, <ns0:hi>Let him mourn for his sin</ns0:hi>? why doth he mourn for his afflictions and plagues, let him rather spend his Tears upon his sins. But the word also signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies the <ns0:hi>guilt of sin,</ns0:hi> or obligation to death, which it layeth men under, <ns0:hi>sin lieth at the door, Gen.</ns0:hi> 4.7. so also <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 20.9. and also any punishment brought upon men for sin, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 4.13. where we translate it punishment. This sense our translators follow. The Prophet then in the person of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> checks himself in his complaints for their punishments from the consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deration, that nothing had befallen them, but what was the just reward of their sins.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 Let us search and try our wayes, and turn again to the LORD <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Seeing God doth not grieve us willingly, nor delight to crush us though we be his Prisoners, and seeing the hand of God is in these things upon us, and that justly to recompense our iniquities into our bosoms, instead of murmuring and fretting against God, which is not reasonable, nor will be of any profit to us, Let us examine our thoughts, words and actions and consider what they have been, and reform, and turn again to the Lord, by aposta<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>izing from whom we have brought these evils upon us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 Let us lift up our heart with <ns0:hi>our</ns0:hi> hands un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to God in the heavens <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Let us apply our selves unto God by Prayer, often expres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed under this notion in Scripture from that gesture ordinarily used in Prayer: and let us not do it in hypocrisie, but joining our hearts with our hands, praying seriously and fervently.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 We have transgressed and have rebelled, thou hast not pardoned <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The Prophet doth not dictate words, but sense to them; teaching them the matter of their Prayer first by way of <ns0:hi>confes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion.</ns0:hi> Sin is called a transgression because it is going aside from the way of Gods precepts, it is called <ns0:hi>Rebellion,</ns0:hi> because it is an act contrary to that Allegiance and duty, which we owe unto God, and the Covenant we have made with him. By pardon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing here is meant, the discharge of the guilty persons from the temporal punishment due for sin (as it is often taken in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture) so it signifies, thou hast plagued us according to the just desert of our sins.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 Thou hast covered with anger <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either thou hast covered thy self with anger, or covered thy own face with anger so as not to look upon us to move thy pity, or (which is more probably the sense) thou hast covered, that is <ns0:hi>overwhelmed us</ns0:hi> with thy wrath.</ns0:note>, and per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />secuted us; <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 2.21.</ns0:note> thou hast slain, thou hast not pitied <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Thou hast pursued us to a fatal ruin without shewing us any pity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 Thou hast covered thy self with a cloud, that <ns0:hi>our</ns0:hi> prayer should not pass through <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">God had covered them with wrath, overwhelming them with afflictions so as they had no way to escape; and whereas in this distress they had nothing else to do, but onely to apply themselves to God, he had hid his face from them, so as they could get no comfortable fight of him, he was as one covered with a Cloud that could not be discerned through that opacous body. What is meant by this cloud, whether, his fixed resolu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion to punish them, or his fresh remembrance of their sins, or his just will to be revenged on them, seems too curiously in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired. The Phrase is a metaphor, and signifies no more than that God would not hear their prayers in their distress.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="45">45 Thou hast made us <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 4.13<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> off-scouring and refuse in the midst of the people <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">That is, thou hast made us to all Nations extreamly con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />temptible, so as they value us no more than the sweepings of their Houses, or the most vile, refuse, and contemp<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="4 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e things imaginable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="46">46 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 2.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> All our enemies have opened their mouths against us <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">That is, to mock, scoff, and reproach us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 24.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Jer. 48.43.</ns0:note> Fear and a snare is come upon us, deso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation and destruction <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">All manner of misery was come upon them. They were seized first with fears and terrors, going to escape these they fell into a snare, or (as it is in the <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi>) into a <ns0:hi>pit,</ns0:hi> out of which they could not get, they were wasted, made desolate and destroyed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="48">48 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 4.19. & 14.17.</ns0:note> Mine eye runneth down with rivers of water, for the destruction of the daughter of my people.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="49">49 Mine eye trickleth down, and ceaseth not, without any intermission <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The Prophet was deeply affected upon the prospect of this evil before it came, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 9.1. and was now much more af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fected when he saw the judgment was come, he wept plen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tifully and constantly, as for their sins which had brought these judgments upon them, so for the judgments themselves as indications of Gods displeasure and wrath against them for their transgressions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="50">50 Till the LORD look down, and behold from heaven <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That is, until the Lord sheweth me some favour. See the Notes on <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="51">51 Mine eye affecteth <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>my <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> mine heart, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>more <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> all.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> because of all the daughters of my city <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The eye and the ear, are those organs of the body, by which the soul exerciseth its senses to bring in all objects whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther pleasant or sad to the understanding to judge of them, ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the judgment of which upon them it is affected, with joy or sorrow, desire or aversation, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and the eye is the chiefest of these because its evidence is more certain, and less subject to deceit. The Prophet, and most of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were eye-witnesses to the Evils which had befallen the <ns0:hi>Iewes,</ns0:hi> and which at present were upon them. So as their hearts were the more affected. The word translated <ns0:hi>affect,</ns0:hi> is by some noted to signifie to <ns0:hi>waste</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>consume,</ns0:hi> which are the effects of a deep affecting the heart with sad and miserable objects.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Our Margent tells us, that it may be also read <ns0:hi>more than all the daugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters of my City</ns0:hi>; according to which the sense is, that he was more affected with the state of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> then the tenderest woman that had lived in it; but it is as well, if not better in this place rendred causally; shewing the reason of his deep afflicti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> all those miseries he had seen fall upon all the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Nation, or upon all the inhabitants of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="52">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:71" />52 Mine enemies chased me sore like a bird, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 35.719. & 69.4. & 109.3. & 119.161.</ns0:note> without cause <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">As Boys beat a Bird from bush to bush, suffering it to rest no where, so mine Enemies to whom I gave no cause pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sued me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="53">53 They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Dungeon seemeth not to be here taken literally for the lowest and nastiest place in Prisons, which probably was the portion but of a few of the <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi>; but metaphorically for the lowest and saddest condition of misery. Their Enemies had brought them into the deepest Miseries to the cutting off of their lives, and as men use to roll great stones upon the mouthes of Dens and Pits, where they have shut up Persons to make them sure from escaping out, so their Enemies had dealt with them, doing what <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ay in them to make their condition re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mediless and desperate.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="54">54 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 69.2. & 124.4, 5.</ns0:note> Waters flowed over mine head <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Afflictions often in Scripture are called waters, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 28.17, 18. and 59.19.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 31.22. Isa. 38.10, 11.</ns0:note> I said, I am cut off <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That is, I am utterly undone, there is no hope for me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="55">55 ¶ <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 130.1.</ns0:note> I called upon thy name, O LORD, out of the low dungeon <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That is, out of my deepest affliction, as <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> out of the <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>elly of Hell, Ionah</ns0:hi> 2.2. I cried unto God, and called upon him for mercy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="56">56 Thou hast heard my voice <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">I in former great afflictions applied my self unto thee, and thou didst hear me.</ns0:note>, hide not thine ear at my breathing, at my cry <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Shew me now the same favour. Our former experiences of Gods goodness to us in hearing our Pray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers, ought to hold up our hands in prayer, and beget a confi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence in us that we persisting in our duty, shall find God the same God, yesterday, this day, and for ever.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="57">57 Thou drewest near in the day <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> I called upon thee <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">There was a time when I was in distress, and called upon thee, and thou didst draw near unto me. God is never far off from any of us, as to his essential presence; nor is it possible that he should, for he filleth all places. But he is said to be near us or far off from us, as he manifests or doth not manifest his goodness to us by acts of gracious Providence; of that draw<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing near the text speaketh. God being infinite in goodness and mercy, is spoken of as absent from those persons and places, where he is not shewing mercy, and present onely there where he sheweth forth his goodness, and to be drawing nigh to them to whom he beginneth to shew Mercy.</ns0:note>: thou saidst, Fear not <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Thou didst incourage me formerly upon my prayer.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="58">58 O LORD, thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Thou hast been wont to take my part against my Enemies, not like a Lawyer by word of mouth, but actually and really pleading my cause.</ns0:note>, thou hast redeemed my life <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Thou hast saved me from many a dan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger which looked fatally upon me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="59">59 O LORD, thou hast seen my wrong <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Thou hast a perfect knowledge of mens perverse, and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />righteous dealings with me at this time.</ns0:note>, judge thou my cause <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Do thou judge be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />twixt me and mine Enemies, and deal with them according to what shall appear just to thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="60">60 Thou hast seen all their vengeance <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Thou hast been a witness to all their fury and rage.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> all their imaginations against me <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">And all their malicious and bloody contrivances against me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="61">61 Thou hast heard their reproach O LORD! <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> all their imaginations against me <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">What ever knowledge men get of things done from their Eye or Ear, thou hast from thy omnisciency, thou knowest not only their malitious actions, but words and thoughts.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="62">62 The lips of those that rose up against me and their device against me all the day <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">That is thou hast observed and noted the motions, or pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ducts of my Enemies lips, and their secret devices, before they came out of their lips.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="63">63 Behold their sitting down, and rising up, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 14.</ns0:note> I am their musick <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">That is at all times when they sit down, and rise up I am their song. Though probably the words have a special refe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence to their sitting down at Feasts, and at their merry meet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings, I am all the subject of their discourse, they spend their time in mocking and scoffing at us, and at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> we are they that make them sport.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="64">64 ¶ <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 23.4.</ns0:note> Render unto them a recompense LORD, according to the work of their hands <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">These three last verses are all but the same general petition, though expressed in various phrases, the Prophet had prayed <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 59. that God would judge his peoples cause, here he pray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth that he would also judge his Enemies, he only desireth justice against them, a recompense of the work of their hands.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="65">65 Give them <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>obstinacy of hea<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>t.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> sorrow of heart <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The word translated sorrow of heart is found no where else in Holy Writ, which makes a certain particular explication of it to be difficult, and hath given Interpreters a strange liber<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty in translating it, <ns0:hi>shield, sorrow, and grief, obstinacy</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>hardness of heart, perplexi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>y, abjection or breaking of heart</ns0:hi>; the best guides we have to direct us in the sense of it are. 1 <ns0:hi>The other things joyned with it, persecution, destruction,</ns0:hi> a recompense according to their works, so that some afflictive evil of an heavy nature is certain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly signified by it. 2. The <ns0:hi>Analogy of Faith</ns0:hi> which restraineth us from wishing or praying for spiritual or eternal evils against our worst Enemies, it therefore probably signifies, such perplexity of mind, and breakings of mind as commonly attend a state of great affliction.</ns0:note>, thy curse unto them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="66">66<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Persecute them and destroy them in anger from under <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 8.3.</ns0:note> the heavens of the LORD <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Bring them to a temporal ruine and destruction. How far such petitions are lawful we have before shewed, in our Notes on <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 69.22, 23, 24. &c. and 109.6, 7, 8, 9, 10. &c. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 11.20. & 15.15. See also <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.22. It is hard to interpret all passages of this nature which we meet with as Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phesies, though some of them are so, and others may be both Prophesies and Prayers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
            </ns0:div>
